(i) **Pascal recurrences.** For $m\ge1$ and every integer $r$,

$$C_{m,r}=q_i^{-r}C_{m-1,r}+q_i^{m-r}C_{m-1,r-1}=q_i^rC_{m-1,r}+q_i^{r-m}C_{m-1,r-1}.$$

(ii) **Symmetry.** For $0\le r\le m$, $C_{m,r}=C_{m,m-r}$.

(iii) **Gauss product formula.** For every $N\ge0$, in the polynomial ring $\mathbb Q(q)[z]$,

$$\prod_{j=0}^{N-1}(1+q_i^{2j}z)=\sum_{r=0}^{N}q_i^{r(N-1)}C_{N,r}z^r.$$

Consequently, for $N\ge1$,

$$\sum_{r=0}^{N}(-1)^rq_i^{r(N-1)}C_{N,r}=0.$$

(iv) **Integrality.** For $0\le r\le m$,

$$C_{m,r}\in q_i^{-r(m-r)}\mathbb Z[q_i^2]\subseteq\mathbb Z[q_i^{\pm1}].$$

Thus every Gaussian quotient is a Laurent polynomial in $q_i$ with integer coefficients, and the Pascal recurrences hold in that Laurent polynomial ring.

A **finite-field hereditary Hall category** is a supplied small
$\mathbb F_q$-linear abelian category $\mathcal A$ with the following
properties:

1. For every pair $M,N$, $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal A}(M,N)$ is a
   finite-dimensional $\mathbb F_q$-vector space and the Yoneda extension
   group $\operatorname{YExt}^1(M,N)$ is finite-dimensional over
   $\mathbb F_q$. Its addition is Baer sum; scalar multiplication by
   $\lambda\in\mathbb F_q$ is pushout along $\lambda\operatorname{id}_N$.
2. For every $M,N$, $\operatorname{YExt}^2(M,N)=0$, where a two-fold
   extension is an exact sequence $0\to N\to E_1\to E_0\to M\to0$
   modulo endpoint-fixed chain-map equivalence
   ([[def-n-fold-yoneda-extension]],
   [[def-equivalence-of-n-fold-extensions]]).
3. Smallness and the finiteness conditions of the Hall definition hold
   ([[def-hall-finitary-abelian-category]]).

Here $\mathbb F_q$-linear means that every Hom set is a vector space and
composition is bilinear. “Hereditary” in this page means exactly the stated
vanishing of Yoneda $\operatorname{Ext}^2$; no projective or injective
resolutions, derived-Ext identification, or choice principle is built into
the definition. Under these conditions the Euler form used below is
$$ \langle[M],[N]\rangle=\dim_{\mathbb F_q}\operatorname{Hom}(M,N) -\dim_{\mathbb F_q}\operatorname{YExt}^1(M,N). $$

Let $\mathcal C$ be an essentially small abelian category
([[def-abelian-category]]). Its set of isomorphism classes is denoted
$\operatorname{Iso}(\mathcal C)$. The **Grothendieck group** of $\mathcal C$ is

$$ G_0(\mathcal C):=\mathbb Z[\operatorname{Iso}(\mathcal C)]\big/\langle e_Y-e_X-e_Z:\ 0\to X\to Y\to Z\to 0\text{ is short exact in }\mathcal C\rangle. $$

where $\mathbb Z[\operatorname{Iso}(\mathcal C)]$ is the free abelian group on
that set ([[def-free-abelian-group]]) and $[X]$ denotes the image of the
generator for the isomorphism class of $X$. Thus the defining relation is
$[Y]=[X]+[Z]$ for every short exact sequence
([[def-exact-sequence-and-short-exact-sequence-in-an-abelian-category]]).
This is the short-exact-sequence group, distinguished below from split
Grothendieck groups of projectives. No free abelian group on the possibly
class-sized collection of all objects is formed. The sequence
$0\to0\to0\to0$ in particular gives $[0]=0$.

Let $\xi$ and $\eta$ be extensions of $M$ by $N$. Form their direct sum, pull it back along the diagonal $\Delta:M\to M\oplus M$, and then push that extension out along the codiagonal $\nabla:N\oplus N\to N$. The resulting extension of $M$ by $N$ is the **Baer sum** $[\xi]+[\eta]$. The direct sum alone has endpoints $N\oplus N$ and $M\oplus M$, so it is only an intermediate construction.

For fixed $M,N$ in an abelian category, assume that the equivalence classes of
extensions of $M$ by $N$ form a set. With Baer sum, that set is an abelian
group. Its zero is the split extension and the inverse of a class is its
pushout along $-1_N$.

At vertex $r$, every positive-length path ending at $r$ has a unique first arrow $a:i\to j$ followed by a path $p:j\to r$. The relation in step 2.2 reduces $(pa)\otimes v$ to $p\otimes V_a(v)$; induction on path length shows the augmentation is surjective and its kernel is generated by those relations. A linear combination of relations has a unique maximal path length; its terms of that length have distinct first-arrow/path/vector indices, so they cannot cancel unless their coefficients vanish. To see directly that every Yoneda two-extension of $V$ by $W$ is zero, write it as $0\to W\to E_1\to E_0\to V\to0$. Projectivity of $P_0(V)$ gives a lift $s:P_0(V)\to E_0$ of its augmentation. The composite of $P_1(V)\to P_0(V)\xrightarrow{s}E_0$ lands in $J=\ker(E_0\to V)=\operatorname{im}(E_1\to E_0)$. Projectivity of $P_1(V)$ lifts it through $E_1\twoheadrightarrow J$ to $t:P_1(V)\to E_1$. The resulting map from the split two-extension $0\to W\to W\oplus P_1(V)\to P_0(V)\to V\to0$ to the given extension is the identity on $W,V$ and commutes with all arrows. The split two-extension is zero in Yoneda $\operatorname{Ext}^2$, so the given extension is zero.

Let $\mathcal A$ be a small finitary abelian category in the sense of
[[def-hall-finitary-abelian-category]], and let $R$ be a commutative ring
with unit. Define the free $R$-module
$$ H_{\mathcal A,R}:=\bigoplus_{[M]\in\operatorname{Iso}(\mathcal A)}R[M], $$
where $[M]$ is a basis symbol for the isomorphism class of $M$. For objects $N,L$, let
$$\operatorname{Mon}_{\mathcal A}(N,L):=\{f\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal A}(N,L): f\text{ is monic}\}.$$
This is a finite set by the Hom condition in
[[def-hall-finitary-abelian-category]]. For $f,g$ in this set, write
$f\sim_N g$ when $g=f\circ u$ for an isomorphism $u:N\to N$; this is an
equivalence relation by [[def-isomorphism-groupoid-and-connected-category]].
The quotient set $\operatorname{Mon}_{\mathcal A}(N,L)/\sim_N$ represents
exactly the subobjects of $L$ isomorphic to $N$: each class gives the usual
subobject class from [[def-subobject-and-quotient-object]], and the mutual-
factorisation theorem says two such monomorphisms give the same subobject
exactly when they differ by such an isomorphism
([[thm-mutual-factorisation-defines-subobject-and-quotient-object-equivalence]]).
Every subobject class with domain isomorphic to $N$ is represented by composing
its monomorphism with an isomorphism from $N$, one class at a time. The
cokernel quotient is independent of that representative by
[[thm-the-quotient-is-independent-of-the-representing-monomorphism]] and
[[def-the-quotient-of-an-object-by-a-subobject]]. Define $g^L_{M,N}$ to be the
number of classes $[f]_{\sim_N}$ for which $\operatorname{coker}(f)\cong M$.
The finiteness lemma below also proves that the resulting product has finite
support. Extend the operation
$$ [M]*[N]:=\sum_{[L]\in\operatorname{Iso}(\mathcal A)}g^L_{M,N}[L] $$
$R$-bilinearly, mapping each natural number coefficient to its multiple of
$1_R$. The order is fixed: the counted short exact sequence is
$$ 0\longrightarrow N\longrightarrow L\longrightarrow M\longrightarrow0. $$

This is the **untwisted Hall product**. It does not use an Euler form, a square
root of a field size, or division by automorphism cardinalities. The finite
coefficient and finite-support claims needed for the operation to define a
bilinear product are established in
[[lem-untwisted-hall-product-finiteness]].

A **small finitary abelian category** for Hall multiplication is a small
abelian category $\mathcal A$ (its object and morphism collections are sets,
by [[def-small-locally-small-and-large-category]]), with abelian structure as
in [[def-abelian-category]], in which the
following sets are finite for every pair of objects $M,N$:

1. $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal A}(M,N)$;
2. $\operatorname{YExt}^{1}_{\mathcal A}(M,N)$, the set of Yoneda classes of
   short exact sequences $0\to N\to E\to M\to0$. Equivalence is the
   one-fold instance of the generated endpoint-fixed chain-map relation in
   [[def-equivalence-of-n-fold-extensions]]: chain maps are the identity on
   $N$ and $M$, and the relation is closed under reflexivity, symmetry and
   transitivity. A short exact sequence and its endpoint order use
   [[def-exact-sequence-and-short-exact-sequence-in-an-abelian-category]],
   [[def-extension-of-an-object-by-an-object-in-an-abelian-category]] and
   [[def-n-fold-yoneda-extension]].

One may instead supply a small skeleton $\mathcal A_0$ of an essentially
small abelian category and perform the construction on $\mathcal A_0$. Here
“essentially small” means that such a small equivalent category is part of the
given data; the construction does not select representatives by an unstated
choice principle. The isomorphism classes $\operatorname{Iso}(\mathcal A_0)$
then form a set.

No $\mathbb F_q$-linear structure, enough projectives or injectives, finite
number of subobjects of every object, or identification with derived
$\operatorname{Ext}^{1}$ is included in this definition. Subobjects are the
monomorphism classes of [[def-subobject-and-quotient-object]], and quotients
are the cokernels specified in [[def-the-quotient-of-an-object-by-a-subobject]].

A sequence of morphisms in an abelian category is **exact** when it is exact at
every interior object in the sense of [[def-exactness-at-a-node]].

In particular, a composable triple
$$0\to A\xrightarrow{i}B\xrightarrow{p}C\to 0$$
is a **short exact sequence** when it is exact at $A$, at $B$, and at $C$.

This page uses the sequence language literally: the definition names exactness
of displayed chains of morphisms, not chain complexes as objects.

$g^L_{M,N}$ is finite and depends only on the isomorphism classes of
$M,N,L$. For fixed $M,N$, only finitely many isomorphism classes $[L]$

$$S(K_h)=K_{-h},\qquad S(E_i)=-E_iK_i,\qquad S(F_i)=-K_i^{-1}F_i.$$

For $n\geq1$, an **$n$-fold extension of $M$ by $N$** is an exact sequence
$$0\longrightarrow N\longrightarrow E_{n-1}\longrightarrow\cdots\longrightarrow E_0\longrightarrow M\longrightarrow0.$$
For $n=1$ this is the preceding notion of a short extension. The left endpoint is always the second Ext variable.

For two $n$-fold extensions with the same endpoints, begin with chain maps between their displayed exact sequences that are the identity on $N$ and $M$. Their reflexive, symmetric, and transitive closure is called **equivalence of $n$-fold extensions**. For $n>1$, this generated relation does not require one isomorphism of all middle terms.

Let
$$
\xi:\qquad 0\longrightarrow N\xrightarrow{i}E\xrightarrow{p}M\longrightarrow0
$$
be an extension in an abelian category.

For a morphism $f:M'\to M$, the **pullback extension** $f^*\xi$ is
$$0\longrightarrow N\xrightarrow{i'}E\times_M M'\xrightarrow{q_2}M'\longrightarrow0,$$
where $q_1:E\times_M M'\to E$ and $q_2:E\times_M M'\to M'$ are the
pullback projections of $p$ and $f$, and $i'$ is the unique map satisfying
$q_1i'=i$ and $q_2i'=0$. Thus pullback is contravariant in the quotient
variable.

For a morphism $g:N\to N'$, the **pushout extension** $g_*\xi$ is
$$0\longrightarrow N'\xrightarrow{j_{N'}}N'\amalg_N E\xrightarrow{p'}M\longrightarrow0,$$
where $j_E:E\to N'\amalg_N E$ and $j_{N'}:N'\to N'\amalg_N E$ are the
pushout maps of $i$ and $g$, and $p'$ is the unique map satisfying
$p'j_E=p$ and $p'j_{N'}=0$. For modules the pushout is
$(N'\oplus E)/\langle(g(n),-i(n)):n\in N\rangle$. Thus pushout is
covariant in the subobject variable. The two displayed sequences are exact
because pullbacks preserve kernels of epimorphisms and pushouts preserve
cokernels of monomorphisms in an abelian category.

An **abelian category** is an additive category ([[def-additive-category]]) in
which every morphism has a kernel and a cokernel, and in which for every
morphism $f$ the canonical comparison morphism

$$\operatorname{coim}(f)\longrightarrow\operatorname{im}(f)$$

constructed in
[[thm-the-canonical-morphism-from-the-coimage-to-the-image-exists-and-is-unique]]
is an isomorphism.

The first two clauses are Grothendieck's AB1, while the invertibility of the
canonical map is this page's working form of AB2.

$$0\longrightarrow N\xrightarrow{i'}E\times_M M'\xrightarrow{q_2}M'\longrightarrow0,$$
where $q_1:E\times_M M'\to E$ and $q_2:E\times_M M'\to M'$ are the
pullback projections of $p$ and $f$, and $i'$ is the unique map satisfying
$q_1i'=i$ and $q_2i'=0$. Thus pullback is contravariant in the quotient
variable.

For a morphism $g:N\to N'$, the **pushout extension** $g_*\xi$ is
$$0\longrightarrow N'\xrightarrow{j_{N'}}N'\amalg_N E\xrightarrow{p'}M\longrightarrow0,$$
where $j_E:E\to N'\amalg_N E$ and $j_{N'}:N'\to N'\amalg_N E$ are the
pushout maps of $i$ and $g$, and $p'$ is the unique map satisfying
$p'j_E=p$ and $p'j_{N'}=0$. For modules the pushout is
$(N'\oplus E)/\langle(g(n),-i(n)):n\in N\rangle$. Thus pushout is
covariant in the subobject variable. The two displayed sequences are exact
because pullbacks preserve kernels of epimorphisms and pushouts preserve
cokernels of monomorphisms in an abelian category.

An **abelian category** is an additive category ([[def-additive-category]]) in
which every morphism has a kernel and a cokernel, and in which for every
morphism $f$ the canonical comparison morphism

$$\operatorname{coim}(f)\longrightarrow\operatorname{im}(f)$$

constructed in
[[thm-the-canonical-morphism-from-the-coimage-to-the-image-exists-and-is-unique]]
is an isomorphism.

The first two clauses are Grothendieck's AB1, while the invertibility of the
canonical map is this page's working form of AB2.

Form their direct sum, pull it back along the diagonal $\Delta:M\to M\oplus M$, and then push that extension out along the codiagonal $\nabla:N\oplus N\to N$. The resulting extension of $M$ by $N$ is the **Baer sum** $[\xi]+[\eta]$. The direct sum alone has endpoints $N\oplus N$ and $M\oplus M$, so it is only an intermediate construction.

extensions of $M$ by $N$ form a set. With Baer sum, that set is an abelian

A **finite-field hereditary Hall category** is a supplied small
$\mathbb F_q$-linear abelian category $\mathcal A$ with the following
properties:

1. For every pair $M,N$, $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal A}(M,N)$ is a
   finite-dimensional $\mathbb F_q$-vector space and the Yoneda extension
   group $\operatorname{YExt}^1(M,N)$ is finite-dimensional over
   $\mathbb F_q$. Its addition is Baer sum; scalar multiplication by
   $\lambda\in\mathbb F_q$ is pushout along $\lambda\operatorname{id}_N$.
2. For every $M,N$, $\operatorname{YExt}^2(M,N)=0$, where a two-fold
   extension is an exact sequence $0\to N\to E_1\to E_0\to M\to0$
   modulo endpoint-fixed chain-map equivalence
   ([[def-n-fold-yoneda-extension]],
   [[def-equivalence-of-n-fold-extensions]]).
3. Smallness and the finiteness conditions of the Hall definition hold
   ([[def-hall-finitary-abelian-category]]).

Here $\mathbb F_q$-linear means that every Hom set is a vector space and
composition is bilinear. “Hereditary” in this page means exactly the stated
vanishing of Yoneda $\operatorname{Ext}^2$; no projective or injective
resolutions, derived-Ext identification, or choice principle is built into
the definition. Under these conditions the Euler form used below is
$$ \langle[M],[N]\rangle=\dim_{\mathbb F_q}\operatorname{Hom}(M,N) -\dim_{\mathbb F_q}\operatorname{YExt}^1(M,N). $$

A **small finitary abelian category** for Hall multiplication is a small
abelian category $\mathcal A$ (its object and morphism collections are sets,
by [[def-small-locally-small-and-large-category]]), with abelian structure as
in [[def-abelian-category]], in which the
following sets are finite for every pair of objects $M,N$:

1. $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal A}(M,N)$;
2. $\operatorname{YExt}^{1}_{\mathcal A}(M,N)$, the set of Yoneda classes of
   short exact sequences $0\to N\to E\to M\to0$. Equivalence is the
   one-fold instance of the generated endpoint-fixed chain-map relation in
   [[def-equivalence-of-n-fold-extensions]]: chain maps are the identity on
   $N$ and $M$, and the relation is closed under reflexivity, symmetry and
   transitivity. A short exact sequence and its endpoint order use
   [[def-exact-sequence-and-short-exact-sequence-in-an-abelian-category]],
   [[def-extension-of-an-object-by-an-object-in-an-abelian-category]] and
   [[def-n-fold-yoneda-extension]].

One may instead supply a small skeleton $\mathcal A_0$ of an essentially
small abelian category and perform the construction on $\mathcal A_0$. Here
“essentially small” means that such a small equivalent category is part of the
given data; the construction does not select representatives by an unstated
choice principle. The isomorphism classes $\operatorname{Iso}(\mathcal A_0)$
then form a set.

No $\mathbb F_q$-linear structure, enough projectives or injectives, finite
number of subobjects of every object, or identification with derived
$\operatorname{Ext}^{1}$ is included in this definition. Subobjects are the
monomorphism classes of [[def-subobject-and-quotient-object]], and quotients
are the cokernels specified in [[def-the-quotient-of-an-object-by-a-subobject]].

Let $E$ be $0\to A\to B\xrightarrow{p}C\to0$ and let $F$ be
$0\to C\to D\to X\to0$ in an abelian category. If their splice is zero in
$\operatorname{YExt}^2(X,A)$, then there is an extension $G$ of $X$ by $B$
whose pushout along $p:B\to C$ is equivalent to $F$. Conversely every such
pushout has zero splice with $E$.

Let $\mathcal C$ be an essentially small abelian category
([[def-abelian-category]]). Its set of isomorphism classes is denoted
$\operatorname{Iso}(\mathcal C)$. The **Grothendieck group** of $\mathcal C$ is

$$ G_0(\mathcal C):=\mathbb Z[\operatorname{Iso}(\mathcal C)]\big/\langle e_Y-e_X-e_Z:\ 0\to X\to Y\to Z\to 0\text{ is short exact in }\mathcal C\rangle. $$

where $\mathbb Z[\operatorname{Iso}(\mathcal C)]$ is the free abelian group on
that set ([[def-free-abelian-group]]) and $[X]$ denotes the image of the
generator for the isomorphism class of $X$. Thus the defining relation is
$[Y]=[X]+[Z]$ for every short exact sequence
([[def-exact-sequence-and-short-exact-sequence-in-an-abelian-category]]).
This is the short-exact-sequence group, distinguished below from split
Grothendieck groups of projectives. No free abelian group on the possibly
class-sized collection of all objects is formed. The sequence
$0\to0\to0\to0$ in particular gives $[0]=0$.

Let $\xi$ and $\eta$ be extensions of $M$ by $N$. Form their direct sum, pull it back along the diagonal $\Delta:M\to M\oplus M$, and then push that extension out along the codiagonal $\nabla:N\oplus N\to N$. The resulting extension of $M$ by $N$ is the **Baer sum** $[\xi]+[\eta]$. The direct sum alone has endpoints $N\oplus N$ and $M\oplus M$, so it is only an intermediate construction.

For fixed $M,N$ in an abelian category, assume that the equivalence classes of
extensions of $M$ by $N$ form a set. With Baer sum, that set is an abelian
group. Its zero is the split extension and the inverse of a class is its
pushout along $-1_N$.

derivations.claim: Kernels and cokernels of representation maps are formed at each vertex; the induced arrow maps satisfy the abelian identities vertexwise. Subrepresentations and quotients of a representation killed by all paths of length $n$ have the same property. If $0\to U\to V\to W\to0$ is vertexwise exact and all length-$r$ paths kill $U$ while all length-$s$ paths kill $W$, then any length-$s$ path sends $V$ into $U$, and the next $r$ arrows kill it. Thus all length-$(r+s)$ paths kill $V$. Consequently nilpotent finite-dimensional representations are closed under kernels, cokernels, and extensions, and form an abelian $k$-linear category. This quantitative bound applies to every extension constructed below.

Fix an ordering of the finite field and of the finite vertex and arrow sets. For each dimension vector $d$, use the fixed spaces $k^{d_i}$ and list the finitely many arrow-matrix tuples. Keep the nilpotent tuples and the lexicographically least member of each orbit under the finite group $\prod_i\operatorname{GL}_{d_i}(k)$. The union over $d\in\mathbb N^{Q_0}$, with all commuting families of matrices as morphisms, is a supplied small skeleton. Isomorphisms to representatives may also be chosen as the least in the corresponding finite matrix sets, so transporting kernels, cokernels, and biproducts to it needs no infinite choice. We use this small abelian model when applying [F1]. Hom spaces are subspaces of the finite-dimensional vector space $\bigoplus_i\operatorname{Hom}_k(V_i,W_i)$.

For fixed nilpotent $V,W$, split a short extension vertexwise, using bases in finitely many finite-dimensional vector spaces. Each arrow $a:i\to j$ then acts on $W_i\oplus V_i$ by the block matrix $\begin{pmatrix}W_a&\xi_a\\0&V_a\end{pmatrix}$ with $\xi_a:V_i\to W_j$. Conversely every tuple $(\xi_a)$ defines a representation extension because a quiver representation has no relations beyond the specified compositions of arrows. It is nilpotent by step 1.1, independently of the tuple. Changing the vertex sections by maps $\theta_i:V_i\to W_i$ changes the tuple by $d(\theta)_a=W_a\theta_i-\theta_jV_a$. Every endpoint-fixed isomorphism is exactly such a change of sections. Hence $\operatorname{YExt}^1(V,W)$ is identified with $\operatorname{coker}\bigl(d:\bigoplus_i\operatorname{Hom}_k(V_i,W_i)\to\bigoplus_{a:i\to j}\operatorname{Hom}_k(V_i,W_j)\bigr)$. Under [F3], Baer sum adds arrow tuples and pushout along $\lambda\operatorname{id}_W$ multiplies them by $\lambda$. This proves that the prescribed extension operations give a finite-dimensional $k$-space.

The vertex representations $S_i$ are simple. Every nonzero nilpotent representation has a subobject isomorphic to some $S_i$: among all nonzero images of nonzero vectors under paths choose one of greatest path length, which exists because sufficiently long paths vanish. Its terminal vector is killed by every outgoing arrow, so its one-dimensional span at that vertex and zero at the other vertices is the required subrepresentation. In a simple representation this is the whole object. Total vector-space dimension strictly decreases on a proper quotient, giving a finite composition series with factors among the $S_i$. Counting vertex dimensions along it and using [F3] gives $[V]=\sum_i\dim_k(V_i)[S_i]$. The dimension-vector map is additive on short exact sequences and sends these classes to the standard basis, so it is inverse to the map $\mathbb Z^{Q_0}\to K_0$ taking that basis to $[S_i]$.

There are finitely many choices, so this does not use the Axiom of Choice. In the resulting coordinates $D_i=C_i\oplus X_i$, its arrow maps have form $\begin{pmatrix}C_a&\xi_a\\0&X_a\end{pmatrix}$. If $s_j:C_j\to B_j$ is the chosen section of $p_j$, put $\widetilde\xi_a=s_j\xi_a$. Define $T_i=B_i\oplus X_i$ and $T_a=\begin{pmatrix}B_a&\widetilde\xi_a\\0&X_a\end{pmatrix}$. These maps define a finite-dimensional quiver representation and an exact sequence $0\to B\to T\to X\to0$.

If length-$r$ paths kill $B$ and length-$s$ paths kill $X$, then length-$(r+s)$ paths kill $T$ by step 1.1. Thus the constructed intermediate object belongs to the nilpotent category, including when $Q$ has oriented cycles. The maps $T_i\to D_i$ given by $(b,x)\mapsto(p_i b,x)$ commute with arrows because $p_j\widetilde\xi_a=\xi_a$ and $p_jB_a=C_ap_i$. They give a surjection $T\to D$ with kernel $A$, and the pushout of $0\to B\to T\to X\to0$ along $p$ is precisely $F$. By [F2] the given two-extension is zero within the nilpotent category itself: the finite zigzag in that lemma involves only finite sums, subquotients, and extensions of these objects, which remain finite-dimensional and nilpotent by step 1.1. Since the original two-extension was arbitrary, all its Yoneda two-extension classes vanish.

Apply step 2.2 to $V=S_i,W=S_j$. If $i\ne j$, the source of $d$ is zero, and its target has one scalar coordinate for each arrow $i\to j$. If $i=j$, that target is zero because $Q$ has no loops. Thus $\dim_k\operatorname{YExt}^1(S_i,S_j)=c_{ij}$ in all cases. Steps 1.1–4.1 verify every condition in [F1], while step 2.3 and this computation prove the remaining assertions. If $Q$ is acyclic then every path has length less than $|Q_0|$, so all finite-dimensional representations are nilpotent; hence the same argument covers precisely the acyclic category in the statement, consistently with [[lem-finite-acyclic-quiver-hall-category-is-hereditary-finitary]].

Let $U_q^-=\bigoplus_{\nu\in Q_+}U_q^-[-\nu]$ be the negative half of the
Drinfeld-Jimbo algebra of a finite symmetrizable Cartan datum with $a_{ii}=2$
([[def-drinfeld-jimbo-quantized-enveloping-algebra]],
[[def-positive-negative-and-toral-quantum-subalgebras]]), with skew derivations
$e_i',e_i''$ ([[def-kashiwara-skew-derivations-on-the-negative-quantum-half]]),
and let $(\ ,\ )$ be a bilinear form on $U_q^-$.

(i) **Existence and symmetry.** A bilinear form with $(1,1)=1$ and
$(F_iP,Q)=(P,e_i'(Q))$ for all $i,P,Q$ exists on $U_q^-$; every normalized
homogeneous form satisfying these conditions is symmetric; and by the
uniqueness of [[def-the-lusztig-kashiwara-bilinear-form-on-the-negative-quantum-half]]
there is exactly one such form. No separate right-adjunction formula for
$(P,QF_i)$ is asserted: in the rank-one subalgebra a formula
$(P,QF_i)=c\,(e_i''P,Q)$ with constant $c$ is false, as the explicit values in
(iv) show.

(ii) **Orthogonality.** $(U_q^-[-\nu],U_q^-[-\mu])=0$ whenever $\nu\ne\mu$.

(iii) **Nondegeneracy.** For every $0\ne x\in U_q^-$ there is $y\in U_q^-$ with
$(x,y)\ne0$; equivalently, the restriction of the form to each
finite-dimensional graded piece $U_q^-[-\nu]$ is nondegenerate.

(iv) **Integrality on the word lattice.** Let $A=\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$
([[def-the-laurent-polynomial-ring]]) and let $W\subseteq U_A^-$ be the
$A$-span of the monomials $F_{i_1}\cdots F_{i_k}$ ($k\ge0$). Then
$W\subseteq U_A^-$ (because $F_i^k=[k]_i!F_i^{(k)}$ and $[k]_i!\in A$), and
$(W,W)\subseteq A$. On the larger divided-power lattice $U_A^-$ the form is
*not* $A$-valued: in the rank-one subalgebra generated by a single $F_i$ one
has, for all $a,b\ge0$,
$$(F_i^{(a)},F_i^{(b)})=\delta_{ab}\frac{q_i^{-a(a-1)/2}}{[a]_i!}=\delta_{ab}\frac{1}{[a]_{q_i^2}!},$$
in particular $(F_i^{(2)},F_i^{(2)})=1/(1+q_i^2)\notin A$; here
$[a]_{q_i^2}!=\prod_{m=1}^a(1+q_i^2+\cdots+q_i^{2(m-1)})$. Globally, with
$A_{\mathrm{loc}}=A[s^{-1}:s\in S]$, the localization of $A$ inverting the
multiplicative set $S$ generated by $\{[r]_i!:i\in I,r\ge1\}$ (equivalently inverting the
Gaussian factorials $[r]_{q_i^2}!$), one has
$(U_A^-,U_A^-)\subseteq A_{\mathrm{loc}}$: divided-power words are word
vectors divided by finite products of these factorials. This is an exact
denominator bound, not an $A$-integrality assertion on $U_A^-$ in this
normalization.

Assume AC ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]), used only through the formal embedding theorem. For an indeterminate $z$, let $H_z^\pm$ be the algebras over $\mathbb C(z)$ presented by the separate symmetric quantum Serre relations, with parameters $z_i=z^{d_i}$.

(i) Each $H^\pm[\pm\alpha]$ is finite free over $R$, and
$$\operatorname{rank}_R H^\pm[\pm\alpha]=\dim_{\mathbb C}U(\mathfrak n^\pm)[\pm\alpha]=\dim_{\mathbb C(z)}H_z^\pm[\pm\alpha].$$
Every family of homogeneous lifts of a basis of the classical component is an $R$-basis. Likewise, homogeneous word expressions with coefficients rational in $z$, regular at $z=1$, which reduce to a classical component basis form a basis of the corresponding generic component. In particular, for a supplied ordered homogeneous basis of $\mathfrak n^\pm$, ordered monomials in any such regular lifts form a generic PBW basis.

(ii) Both formal halves are graded braided Hopf algebras. Their generators are primitive, their counits kill positive height, and their tensor squares use
$$ (u\otimes v)(u'\otimes v')=q^{-\langle\deg u',\deg v\rangle}uu'\otimes vv',\qquad \langle\epsilon_i,\epsilon_j\rangle=d_i a_{ij},$$
with negative degrees for $H^-$. The word pairing restricts and descends to a nondegenerate $K$-valued pairing $H^+\times H^-$ with $\langle e_i,f_j\rangle=\delta_{ij}/(\hbar d_i)$ and $\langle1,1\rangle=1$. It is zero on unequal opposite degrees and satisfies the braided Hopf adjunctions
$$\langle x,yy'\rangle=\sum\langle x_{(1)},y\rangle\langle x_{(2)},y'\rangle,\qquad\langle xx',y\rangle=\sum\langle x,y_{(1)}\rangle\langle x',y_{(2)}\rangle.$$
The generic halves have the same braided Hopf structures and a nondegenerate $\mathbb C(z)$-valued pairing normalized by $\langle e_i,f_j\rangle_z=\delta_{ij}/(z_i-z_i^{-1})$. All generic assertions also hold for the corresponding $\mathbb Q(z)$-presentations and their rational pairing, with the PBW lift clause using bases of the rational classical Serre form.

Let $\psi$ (the bar involution) and $\tau$ (the contravariant anti-involution) be
the semilinear maps of
[[lem-quantum-serre-relations-are-stable-under-the-chevalley-involutions]], so
that $\psi(q)=q^{-1}$, $\psi(E_i)=E_i$, $\psi(F_i)=F_i$, $\psi(K_h)=K_h^{-1}$
and $\tau(q)=q^{-1}$, $\tau(E_i)=F_i$, $\tau(F_i)=E_i$, $\tau(K_h)=K_h^{-1}$,
with $\tau$ anti-multiplicative. Let $A=\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$ and let $U_A$ be
the Lusztig divided-power integral form with its generators $E_i^{(r)}$,
$F_i^{(r)}$, $K_h^{\pm1}$ and toral binomials $T_{i,c,t}$
([[def-lusztig-divided-power-integral-form]]). Then $\psi(U_A)=U_A$ and
$\tau(U_A)=U_A$. Explicitly, on the generators,

$$\psi(E_i^{(r)})=E_i^{(r)},\quad \psi(F_i^{(r)})=F_i^{(r)},\quad \psi(K_h)=K_h^{-1},\quad \psi(T_{i,c,t})=T_{i,c,t},$$

$$\tau(E_i^{(r)})=F_i^{(r)},\quad \tau(F_i^{(r)})=E_i^{(r)},\quad \tau(K_h)=K_h^{-1},\quad \tau(T_{i,c,t})=T_{i,c,t}.$$

In particular both maps restrict to bijections of $U_A$: $\psi$ to a semilinear
algebra involution of $U_A$ and $\tau$ to a semilinear anti-involution of
$U_A$, while $q^{\pm1}\in A$ keeps all coefficients in $A$. These are the two
involutions under which the bar lattice and the contravariant duality of the
later constructions are taken; neither formula is the Chevalley involution
$\omega$, which changes signs, exchanges the two halves and is treated in
[[lem-quantum-serre-relations-are-stable-under-the-chevalley-involutions]].
No choice is used.

Fix a symmetrizable Cartan datum and $i\in I$, and use the conventions of [[def-quantum-integers-factorials-and-divided-powers-at-q-i]]. Write $C_{m,r}:=\binom{m}{r}_i$, with $C_{m,r}=0$ when $r<0$ or $r>m$.

(i) **Pascal recurrences.** For $m\ge1$ and every integer $r$,

$$C_{m,r}=q_i^{-r}C_{m-1,r}+q_i^{m-r}C_{m-1,r-1}=q_i^rC_{m-1,r}+q_i^{r-m}C_{m-1,r-1}.$$

(ii) **Symmetry.** For $0\le r\le m$, $C_{m,r}=C_{m,m-r}$.

(iii) **Gauss product formula.** For every $N\ge0$, in the polynomial ring $\mathbb Q(q)[z]$,

$$\prod_{j=0}^{N-1}(1+q_i^{2j}z)=\sum_{r=0}^{N}q_i^{r(N-1)}C_{N,r}z^r.$$

Consequently, for $N\ge1$,

$$\sum_{r=0}^{N}(-1)^rq_i^{r(N-1)}C_{N,r}=0.$$

(iv) **Integrality.** For $0\le r\le m$,

$$C_{m,r}\in q_i^{-r(m-r)}\mathbb Z[q_i^2]\subseteq\mathbb Z[q_i^{\pm1}].$$

Thus every Gaussian quotient is a Laurent polynomial in $q_i$ with integer coefficients, and the Pascal recurrences hold in that Laurent polynomial ring.

Let $Q$ be a finite loopless quiver over $\mathbb F_q$. If $Q$ has oriented

representations; if $Q$ is acyclic, take all finite-dimensional
representations. This category is a small finite-field hereditary Hall
category. Its simple objects are $S_i$, $K_0\cong\mathbb Z^{Q_0}$ by dimension
vector, and $\dim_{\mathbb F_q}\operatorname{YExt}^1(S_i,S_j)=c_{ij}$ for
arrows $i\to j$.

[[def-euler-twisted-hall-algebra]]. For a basis object $R$, let
$P^R_{M,N}$ count endpoint-labelled exact sequences
$0\to N\to R\to M\to0$, and put $a_R=|\operatorname{Aut}(R)|$. Define the
**coefficientwise completed tensor space**
$$ H_{\mathcal A,\nu}\widehat\otimes H_{\mathcal A,\nu} =\prod_{([M],[N])}\mathbb Q(\nu)\,([M]\otimes[N]), $$
the space of all coefficient functions on ordered pairs of isomorphism
classes. Define the Green coproduct and counit by
$$ \Delta'([R])=\sum_{[M],[N]} \nu^{\chi_0(M,N)}\frac{P^R_{M,N}}{a_R}[M]\otimes[N], \qquad \epsilon([R])=\begin{cases}1,&R\cong0,\\0,&R\not\cong0.\end{cases} $$
Each coefficient is finite; the sum need not have finite support. On finite
pure tensors define the **Euler-twisted tensor multiplication** by
$$ ([X]\otimes[Y])\cdot([Z]\otimes[W]) =\nu^{\chi_0(Y,Z)+\chi_0(Z,Y)}([X]\star[Z])\otimes([Y]\star[W]). $$
It is extended to completed tensors only when every output coefficient is a
finite sum. No algebra structure on the whole completion is asserted; this
finite-convergence condition is proved for products of Green images below.

On the direct-sum Hall space define
$$ ([M],[N])_G=\frac{\delta_{[M],[N]}}{a_M}. $$
This bilinear form is nondegenerate over $\mathbb Q(\nu)$ and satisfies
$$ ([M]\star[N],[R])_G =([M]\otimes[N],\Delta'([R]))_{G\otimes G}, $$
where the tensor pairing is the product of the two Green pairings.

For a finite-field hereditary Hall category, products of Green images converge
coefficientwise and
$$ \Delta'([M]\star[N])=\Delta'([M])\cdot\Delta'([N]) $$
in the completion of [[def-green-hall-completion-and-coproduct]], where the
target multiplication is the stated Euler-twisted tensor multiplication. The
coproduct is coassociative and counital by
[[lem-green-hall-coproduct-is-coassociative]]. It is not asserted that the
whole completion is an algebra.

u^{-1}$ and sending $X_{i,n}$ to $u_i^n/[n]_{
u^{-1}}!$ in $C_K$. All denominators are nonzero because $
u>1$. The latter map has image $C_K$, since $X_{i,1}$ maps to $u_i$.

For homogeneous $P,R\in\mathcal T$ of degree $\alpha$, the Hall pairing of their second images is $(\Phi(P),\Phi(R))_H=(Q-1)^{-\operatorname{ht}\alpha}\left.B_t(P(F),R(F))ight|_{t=
u^{-1}}$. Indeed first take ordinary words: both sides are determined by the same primitive coproduct and tensor twist, the same simple pairings and the vacuum value, by peeling a first letter through the adjunction. The twists coincide because $(
u^{-1})^{-(\alpha, eta)}=
u^{(\alpha, eta)}$, and the height factor changes each generator norm from $1$ to $1/(Q-1)$. The formula then extends to divided words by their scalar denominators and to $A$-linear combinations by bilinearity and evaluation of coefficients. All expressions are evaluable by [F2]. Unequal degrees pair to zero on both sides.

Let $S$ be a finite set with Coxeter matrix $m$ and diagram $\Gamma$
([[def-cg-coxeter-diagram-components-and-finite-type]]), $W$ the presented group
with length $\ell$ ([[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]]),
$V=\mathbb R^S$ with Coxeter form $B$ and cosine matrix
$C=(B(e_s,e_t))_{s,t\in S}=(-\cos(\pi/m(s,t)))_{s,t}$
([[def-cg-real-coxeter-form-and-reflection]]), with $\cos(\pi/\infty):=1$ in this matrix notation.

**(1) Irreducible case.** If $\Gamma$ is connected, then $W$ is finite if and
only if $\Gamma$ is isomorphic as a labelled graph
([[def-graph-isomorphism-and-complement]]) to one of the following **standard
diagrams**:

- $A_n$, $n\ge1$: a path on $n$ vertices, all edges labelled $3$;
- $B_n$, $n\ge2$: a path on $n$ vertices whose labels are $3,\dots,3,4$ (one
  edge of label $4$, at an end);
- $D_n$, $n\ge4$: the star with one degree-$3$ vertex and three arms of
  $1,1,n-3$ vertices, all edges labelled $3$;
- $E_6$, $E_7$, $E_8$: the stars with arms of $1,2,2$; $1,2,3$; $1,2,4$ vertices,
  all edges labelled $3$;
- $F_4$: the path on four vertices with labels $3,4,3$;
- $H_3$: the path on three vertices with labels $3,5$, and $H_4$: the path on
  four vertices with labels $3,3,5$;
- $I_2(m)$, $3\le m<\infty$: two vertices joined by a single edge labelled $m$.

**(2) Reducible case.** For an arbitrary finite $S$, with components of $\Gamma$
on the vertex sets $S_1,\dots,S_k$, the group $W$ is finite if and only if every
component $\Gamma_{S_i}$ is one of the diagrams of (1); in that case
$W\cong W_{S_1}\times\cdots\times W_{S_k}$
([[lem-cg-diagram-products-and-invariant-form-comparison]] (1),
[[def-external-direct-product-of-groups]]). Thus the finite Coxeter systems are
exactly the direct products of the irreducible types listed in (1).

**(3) Positivity of the listed diagrams.** For every diagram $\Gamma$ of the
list (1) the form $B$ is positive definite. In more detail: every proper
principal submatrix of the matrix of $B$ is a block diagonal matrix whose blocks
are matrices of listed diagrams of smaller rank, and the determinant of the full
$n\times n$ cosine matrix of each listed diagram, multiplied by $2^n$ (i.e.
$\det(2C)$), is
$$A_n: n+1,\quad B_n: 2,\quad D_n: 4,\quad E_6: 3,\ E_7: 2,\ E_8: 1,\quad F_4: 1,\quad H_3: 3-\sqrt5,\quad H_4: \frac{7-3\sqrt5}2,\quad I_2(m): 4\sin^2(\pi/m),$$
all of which are positive. Hence $B$ is positive definite for each listed
diagram (Sylvester's criterion;
[[thm-sylvesters-criterion-for-positive-definiteness]]), and by (1) of
[[thm-cg-finite-type-positive-definite-criterion]] each such diagram defines a
finite Coxeter group.

**(4) Coincidences.** As Coxeter systems one has $A_2=I_2(3)$,
$B_2=C_2=I_2(4)$ and $G_2=I_2(6)$; more generally with the usual naming
conventions $A_1=B_1$ (the one-vertex diagram), $A_3=D_3$ (the path on three
vertices), $H_2=I_2(5)$, and $A_1\times A_1=I_2(2)$ if the notation $I_2(m)$ is
extended to $m=2$, the disconnected two-vertex diagram (no edge, since $m=2$
draws no edge). Apart from these identifications the diagrams of (1) are
pairwise non-isomorphic, and the classification list is therefore the
duplicate-free list $A_n$ ($n\ge1$), $B_n$ ($n\ge2$), $D_n$ ($n\ge4$),
$E_6,E_7,E_8,F_4,H_3,H_4$ and $I_2(m)$ with $m\ge3$, $m\notin\{3,4\}$,
where $I_2(3),I_2(4)$ are also written $A_2,B_2$ and $I_2(5),I_2(6)$ are also
written $H_2,G_2$.

Let $S$ be a finite set with Coxeter matrix $m$, presented group $W$, length
function $\ell$ and diagram $\Gamma$
([[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]],
[[def-cg-coxeter-diagram-components-and-finite-type]]); let $V=\mathbb R^S$
carry the Coxeter form $B$ with reflections $r_a$
([[def-cg-real-coxeter-form-and-reflection]]), let
$\rho:W\to\mathrm{GL}(V)$ be the canonical reflection homomorphism
([[def-cg-canonical-reflection-homomorphism]]), and let $V^*$ be the algebraic
dual with its dual action, the closed chamber $C$ and its interior $C^\circ$
([[def-cg-dual-chambers-and-reflection-hyperplanes]],
[[lem-cg-dual-action-and-chamber-faces-exist]]).

**(1) Finiteness criterion.** $W$ is finite if and only if $B$ is positive
definite ([[def-definiteness-inertia-and-signature-data-over-the-reals]]).

**(2) The dual form.** Assume $B$ is positive definite. Then
$b:V\to V^*$, $b(v):=B(v,\cdot)$, is a linear isomorphism, and
$B^*(f,g):=B(b^{-1}f,b^{-1}g)$ defines a positive definite symmetric bilinear
form $B^*$ on $V^*$; for every $w\in W$ the dual map $\rho^*(w)$ preserves
$B^*$: $B^*(w\cdot f,w\cdot g)=B^*(f,g)$ for all $f,g\in V^*$.

**(3) Isolation of the identity and discreteness.** For every $f\in C^\circ$
the set $\Omega_f:=\{h\in\mathrm{GL}(V^*):h\cdot f\in C^\circ\}$ is an open
neighbourhood of $\mathrm{id}_{V^*}$ in $\mathrm{GL}(V^*)$ and
$\Omega_f\cap\rho^*(W)=\{\mathrm{id}\}$. Consequently $\rho^*(W)$ is a discrete
subgroup of $\mathrm{GL}(V^*)$, and $\rho(W)$ is a discrete subgroup of
$\mathrm{GL}(V)$. This clause uses no positive definiteness of $B$.

Let $S$ be a finite set, $m$ a Coxeter matrix, $W$ the presented group ([[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]]), $V=\mathbb R^S$ with Coxeter form $B$, the reflections $r_a$ ([[def-cg-real-coxeter-form-and-reflection]]), the canonical reflection homomorphism $\rho:W\to\mathrm{GL}(V)$, the root system $\Phi=\{\rho(w)e_s\}$, the reflections $T$, and the positive cone $V_+=\{\sum_s\lambda_se_s:\lambda_s\ge0\}$ ([[def-cg-canonical-reflection-homomorphism]]); every root satisfies $B(\alpha,\alpha)=1$ ([[lem-cg-reflection-representation-descends-and-root-norms]] (3)). Let $C,C^\circ$ be the chamber and its interior of the dual action and put $B_s:=\{f\in V^*:f(e_s)>0\}$ ([[def-cg-dual-chambers-and-reflection-hyperplanes]]).

**(1) Sign criterion for the cone.** For $v\in V$: $v\in V_+\setminus\{0\}$ if and only if $f(v)>0$ for every $f\in C^\circ$.

**(2) Roots have a sign.** Every root $\alpha\in\Phi$ lies in $V_+\setminus\{0\}$ or in $-V_+\setminus\{0\}$, and not in both. Hence, with
$$\Phi_+:=\Phi\cap V_+,\qquad \Phi_-:=\Phi\cap(-V_+),$$
one has $\Phi=\Phi_+\sqcup\Phi_-$, $\Phi_-=-\Phi_+$, $e_s\in\Phi_+$ for every $s\in S$, and for every $w\in W$ and $s\in S$
$$\rho(w)e_s\in\Phi_+\iff w^{-1}C^\circ\subseteq B_s,\qquad \rho(w)e_s\in\Phi_-\iff w^{-1}C^\circ\subseteq sB_s.$$
In particular $f(\alpha)>0$ for all $f\in C^\circ$ when $\alpha\in\Phi_+$, and $f(\alpha)<0$ for all $f\in C^\circ$ when $\alpha\in\Phi_-$.

**(3) Simple reflections act on positive roots.** For every $s\in S$,
$$r_s(\Phi_+\setminus\{e_s\})=\Phi_+\setminus\{e_s\},\qquad r_se_s=-e_s,\qquad r_s\Phi=\Phi;$$
equivalently $r_s\Phi_+=(\Phi_+\setminus\{e_s\})\cup\{-e_s\}$.

Let $E$ be a finite-dimensional real vector space with a positive definite symmetric bilinear form $(\ ,\ )$. A **finite reduced crystallographic root system** is a finite subset $\Phi\subseteq E\setminus\{0\}$ spanning $E$, such that for every $\alpha,\beta\in\Phi$ the integer $\langle\beta,\alpha^\vee\rangle=2(\beta,\alpha)/(\alpha,\alpha)$ is integral, the reflection $s_\alpha(x)=x-\langle x,\alpha^\vee\rangle\alpha$ preserves $\Phi$, and the only scalar multiples of $\alpha$ in $\Phi$ are $\alpha,-\alpha$. The **Weyl group** $W$ is the subgroup of linear isometries of $E$ generated by these reflections. A **root reflection** means one of the $s_\alpha$. The empty root system on $E=0$ is allowed, with $W=\{1\}$.

Choose $t\in E$ such that $(t,\alpha)\ne0$ for every root. Put $\Phi^+=\{\alpha:(t,\alpha)>0\}$ and $\Phi^-=-\Phi^+$. A positive root is **simple** if it is not the sum of two positive roots. The following positive-root lemma proves that the simple roots form a basis $\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_r$ and that the simple reflections $s_i=s_{\alpha_i}$ generate $W$; no such assertion is assumed by this definition. Once proved, let $\ell(w)$ be the least number of simple reflections in a word for $w$ and let $\operatorname{Inv}(w)=\{\alpha\in\Phi^+:w\alpha\in\Phi^-\}$. A word is reduced if its length equals $\ell(w)$.

Identify $E$ with its dual by the displayed form, so $\alpha^\vee=2\alpha/(\alpha,\alpha)$. The root and coroot groups are $Q=\sum_{\alpha\in\Phi}\mathbb Z\alpha$ and $Q^\vee=\sum_{\alpha\in\Phi}\mathbb Z\alpha^\vee$. The **weight group** is $P=\{\lambda\in E:(\lambda,\alpha^\vee)\in\mathbb Z\text{ for all }\alpha\in\Phi\}$; the positive-root lemma proves it is a lattice with basis the vectors dual to the simple coroots. Put $Q_+=\sum_i\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\alpha_i$, and write $\mu\le\lambda$ when $\lambda-\mu\in Q_+$. The open and closed positive chambers are $\mathcal C=\{x:(x,\alpha_i)>0\text{ for all }i\}$ and $\overline{\mathcal C}=\{x:(x,\alpha_i)\ge0\text{ for all }i\}$. A weight is dominant if it belongs to $P\cap\overline{\mathcal C}$. More generally chambers are the connected components of $E\setminus\bigcup_{\alpha\in\Phi}\alpha^\perp$. The closed-chamber representative and stabilizer assertions are proved later, not included as axioms.

For the preceding finite reduced crystallographic root system, regular vectors $t$ exist, $W$ is finite, and the simple positive roots are a basis of $E$. Every root has integral coordinates in this basis of one sign. Each $s_i$ permutes $\Phi^+\setminus\{\alpha_i\}$ and sends $\alpha_i$ to $-\alpha_i$. The simple reflections generate $W$, and every root is the image of a simple root under their group. The simple coroots similarly form an integral basis of the coroot group, and $P$ is the lattice generated by their dual basis; $W$ preserves $Q,Q^\vee,P$. All assertions are choice-free, including rank zero.

Let $Q$ be a finite acyclic quiver and $k=\mathbb F_q$. A representation is
finite-dimensional at every vertex, with one linear map for each arrow. The
category $\operatorname{Rep}_k(Q)$ is a small hereditary finitary abelian
category in the sense of
[[def-finite-field-hereditary-hall-category]]. Its simple objects are the
vertex representations $S_i$, its Grothendieck group is freely generated by
$[S_i]$ and is isomorphic to $\mathbb Z^{Q_0}$, and
$$ \dim_k\operatorname{YExt}^1(S_i, S_j)=c_{ij}, $$
where $c_{ij}$ is the number of arrows $i\to j$.
For any two representations $V,W$, its Euler form is explicitly
$$ \langle[V],[W]\rangle =\sum_{i\in Q_0}\dim V_i\dim W_i -\sum_{a:i\to j}\dim V_i\dim W_j. $$

Let $A$ be any unital associative $\mathbb Z$-graded algebra over a field $k$.
Every finite-dimensional graded left $A$-module is a finite direct sum of
nonzero graded-indecomposable modules (modules not decomposable as a direct sum
of two nonzero graded submodules), with the zero module represented by the
empty sum. If a module has two such decompositions, their summands have the same
finite multiset of isomorphism classes in $\operatorname{GrMod}_0(A)$, that is,
up to degree-zero graded isomorphism
([[def-graded-ring-module-bimodule-and-internal-shift]]). Ungraded isomorphism
classes are not substituted.

derivations.claim: At a sink $i$, write $f_M:\bigoplus_{j\to i}M_j\to M_i$ for the incoming map. A complement to its image is an $S_i$ direct summand, because there are no outgoing arrows. Conversely an $S_i$ summand makes $f_M$ nonsurjective. Thus absence of this summand is exactly surjectivity. After reflection the outgoing map from the new $i$-space is the kernel inclusion and is injective, the source analogue of this condition. Taking its cokernel recovers $M_i$ and every incoming arrow. Conversely the kernel of the source cokernel recovers the source module. These constructions on morphisms give mutually inverse full equivalences on the specified subcategories.

In a short exact sequence whose terms have surjective incoming maps, apply the snake lemma to their incoming-map diagram. The cokernels vanish, so the kernel sequence is exact. Such representations are extension closed: if the outer incoming maps are onto, the middle one is onto by a lift followed by correction from the subobject. The same statements hold dually for injective outgoing maps. Thus the two equivalences are exact for these inherited exact structures and identify the entire $\operatorname{Ext}^1$ groups between their objects, since all extension middle terms stay in the subcategory. Tensoring kernels or cokernels with a field extension is exact, proving field-extension compatibility. At a reflected vertex their dimension vector changes by $s_i d$, since the new coordinate is $\sum_{j\sim i}d_j-d_i$.

For the classification assertions now assume finite ADE type. Choose a sink ordering $1,\ldots,r$ of a connected component, so arrows initially go from higher to lower labels. Reflect each vertex once in this order and repeat; the orientation returns after every full pass, since each edge has been reversed at both endpoints. Let $C=s_r\cdots s_1$ be its action on dimension columns. If $y=Cx$, the successive coordinate updates give $y_i=-x_i+\sum_{j<i,j\sim i}y_j+\sum_{j>i,j\sim i}x_j$. Put $L=I-B_-$ with $B_-$ the strict lower adjacency matrix. These equations say $Ly=-L^t x$, so $C=-L^{-1}L^t$ and $1-C=L^{-1}(L+L^t)=L^{-1}A$. The Cartan matrix $A$ is nonsingular by [F1]. Since $C$ lies in the finite Weyl group, some $h>0$ has $C^h=1$; then $(1-C)\sum_{j=0}^{h-1}C^j=0$ and consequently $\sum_{j=0}^{h-1}C^j=0$.

Apply this repeated sink process to an indecomposable. Unless it is the simple at the currently reflected sink, step 1.1 preserves it as a nonzero indecomposable and step 2.1 reflects its dimension. If it never became that simple, every $C^j d$ would be a nonnegative nonzero dimension vector. Their sum over one order of $C$ cannot be zero, contradicting step 3.1. Thus it reaches a sink simple at a finite step. Reflecting the dimension backwards proves $d$ is a positive root. The exact equivalences preserve endomorphism rings and self-$\operatorname{Ext}^1$; for a sink simple these are $k$ and $0$. Repeating over an algebraic closure and using field-extension compatibility shows absolute indecomposability.

Conversely begin with any positive root $d$ and the same repeated sink order. A positive root remains positive under a step unless it is the simple root being reflected, by [F1]. If it never reached that simple root, all its full-pass transforms would stay positive, again contradicting the zero Coxeter sum in step 3.1. Stop just before its first negative transform and put the corresponding sink simple there. Reverse the preceding reflection functors. At every reverse step its root is not the simple at that source, so step 1.1 applies and constructs a nonzero indecomposable of the required dimension. If two indecomposables had this dimension, their deterministic dimension path reaches the same terminal simple at the same first negative step. The inverse equivalences then make them isomorphic. This proves existence and uniqueness for every positive root, including arbitrary finite base fields.

Order indecomposables by their first stopping time in the repeated sink process. Distinct ones cannot stop at the same time, since the terminal simple and inverse functors would then coincide. If $M_i$ stops before $M_j$, transport both to just before the earlier stopping time. The former is a sink simple $S_s$, the latter has onto incoming map and is not $S_s$. Any map from that latter module to $S_s$ is a functional vanishing on the image of its incoming map, so is zero; and $\operatorname{Ext}^1(S_s,-)=0$ because $S_s$ is projective at a sink. The Hom and Ext identifications in steps 1.1 and 2.1 transport these two vanishings back. Distinct connected components have both Hom and Ext zero, so concatenate their orders. The finite enumeration and root constructions use only the inherited Choice; [F3] supplies the direct-sum interpretation.

Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from finite-root suppliers. Let $Q$ be a finite acyclic quiver and $k=\mathbb F_q$. At a sink $i$
define the reflection functor on a representation $M$ by replacing $M_i$ with
$\ker(\bigoplus_{j\to i}M_j\to M_i)$ and reversing the incident arrows
using its kernel projections. At a source use the dual cokernel functor.
These are inverse exact equivalences between the full subcategories with no
$S_i$ direct summand. They commute with field extension.

If the underlying graph is a finite ADE forest, the dimension map gives a bijection from the indecomposable $kQ$-modules
to the positive roots of the componentwise finite root system. Every
indecomposable is absolutely indecomposable, has endomorphism ring $k$ and
self-$\operatorname{Ext}^1=0$. There is an ordering $M_1,\ldots,M_m$ of
these indecomposables with
$$\operatorname{Hom}(M_j,M_i)=0,\qquad \operatorname{Ext}^1(M_i,M_j)=0\qquad(i<j).$$
Here representations are finite-dimensional; there are no oriented cycles,
so path nilpotence is automatic.

Let $A$ be any unital associative $\mathbb Z$-graded algebra over a field $k$.
Every finite-dimensional graded left $A$-module is a finite direct sum of
nonzero graded-indecomposable modules (modules not decomposable as a direct sum
of two nonzero graded submodules), with the zero module represented by the
empty sum. If a module has two such decompositions, their summands have the same
finite multiset of isomorphism classes in $\operatorname{GrMod}_0(A)$, that is,

Let $\mathcal A$ be a finite-field hereditary Hall category over
$\mathbb F_q$, and choose the positive square root $\nu=\sqrt q$. For
objects $M,N$, put
$\chi_0(M,N)=\dim_{\mathbb F_q}\operatorname{Hom}(M,N)-
\dim_{\mathbb F_q}\operatorname{YExt}^1(M,N)$. This integer depends only on
the isomorphism classes of $M,N$. At this point $\chi_0$ is only an
object-level exponent; additivity on $K_0$ and the resulting bicharacter are
separate proof obligations. The coefficient field is $\mathbb Q(\nu)$. The
**Euler-twisted Hall algebra** is the graded
vector
space
$$ H_{\mathcal A,\nu}=\bigoplus_{[M]}\mathbb Q(\nu)[M],\qquad \deg[M]=[M]\in K_0(\mathcal A), $$
with bilinear operation
$$ [M]\star[N] =\nu^{\chi_0(M,N)}\sum_{[L]}g^L_{M,N}[L], $$
where [[def-untwisted-hall-algebra]] fixes
$0\to N\to L\to M\to0$. This operation is distinct from the untwisted
product: its field, Euler exponent and square-root parameter are additional
data. Finite support and associativity are verified in the following items.

Let $\mathcal A$ be a finite-field hereditary Hall category and let
$K_0=K_0(\mathcal A)$. Put
$([\alpha],[\beta])=\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle+
\langle\beta,\alpha\rangle$. The **extended Hall algebra** is the vector
space $\widetilde H=\mathbb Q(\nu)[K_0]\otimes H_{\mathcal A,\nu}$ with
basis $k_\alpha[M]$ and multiplication
$$ (k_\alpha[M])(k_\beta[N]) =\nu^{-(\beta,[M])}k_{\alpha+\beta}([M]\star[N]). $$
The notation is left-torus normal order: $k_\alpha[M]$ is the actual product of the torus and Hall elements. Thus moving $k_\beta$ past $[M]$ contributes $\nu^{-(\beta,[M])}$. Equivalently, $k_\alpha k_\beta=k_{\alpha+\beta}$ and
$k_\alpha[M]k_\alpha^{-1}=\nu^{(\alpha,[M])}[M]$. Associativity follows
from the bilinearity of the symmetric Euler form and the associative Hall
product; the toral action is checked in
[[lem-extended-hall-torus-action-is-well-defined]].

If $\mathcal A$ has a specified set of simple objects $\{S_i\}$, the
**composition subalgebra** is the subalgebra of $H_{\mathcal A,\nu}$
generated by $[S_i]$. Its extension by all $k_\alpha$ is the **extended
composition subalgebra**.

derivations.claim: By [F1], every extension of $M_i^{\oplus a}$ by $M_j^{\oplus b}$ for $i\le j$ splits. Hence an ordered Hall product of such blocks is a nonzero scalar multiple of their direct sum: the only possible middle object is the direct sum, and at least its canonical summand inclusion contributes to the positive integer Hall count. Its Euler factor is a nonzero power of $\nu$. This proves that whenever the individual indecomposable classes in a sum have been generated, the class of that sum is generated. In particular $[S_i^{\oplus a}]$ is a nonzero scalar multiple of $[S_i]^a$, since there are no self-extensions at a loopless vertex.

Number the vertices topologically, with arrows from earlier to later vertices. For a dimension vector $d$, the product $[d_1S_1]\star\cdots\star[d_rS_r]$ has the same nonzero coefficient on every object of dimension $d$. Indeed it counts the unique descending filtration whose successive quotients are supported at these vertices: the subobject after each step is the entire representation on the remaining terminal vertex set and zero on the preceding vertices. This is a subrepresentation because arrows never go from a terminal vertex to an earlier one. There are no choices of subspaces within a vertex block. All Euler factors depend only on $d$, so their product is a common nonzero scalar. There are finitely many objects in the degree, since there are finitely many arrow matrices over $k$.

Induct on the total dimension of an indecomposable $M$. The one-dimensional case is a vertex simple. For larger dimension $d$, [F1] gives exactly one indecomposable of dimension $d$. Every other object of that degree is a direct sum of smaller-dimensional indecomposables by [F2]; its class is generated by induction and step 1.1. The simple word in step 2.1 is generated by step 1.1. Subtract all its other degree-$d$ classes and divide by its nonzero coefficient to isolate $[M]$. This proves generation of every indecomposable, and step 1.1 then proves generation of every object. The composition and extended conclusions are exactly their definitions in [F3]. Across distinct components the cross Euler form, Hom and Ext are zero, so the same argument covers every finite ADE forest, including the empty one.

Let $\mathbb F_q$ be a finite field of order $q$ and let $E$ be a finite field
having $\mathbb F_q$ as a subfield, with $[E:\mathbb F_q]=n$
([[def-extension-degree-and-finite-extension]]). Then $E/\mathbb F_q$ is a finite
Galois extension ([[def-finite-galois-extension-and-galois-group]]) and

$$\operatorname{Gal}(E/\mathbb F_q)=\langle\sigma_q\rangle$$

is cyclic of order $n$, generated by the relative Frobenius
$\sigma_q\colon x\mapsto x^{q}$
([[def-relative-frobenius-of-a-finite-field-extension]]).
The multiplicative group $F^\times=F\setminus\{0\}$ of every finite field $F$ is cyclic.
Let $G$ be a group and $K$ a field. Every finite family of distinct group homomorphisms $G\to K^\times$ is linearly independent over $K$ as a family of functions.

Let $A$ be any unital associative $\mathbb Z$-graded algebra over a field $k$.
Every finite-dimensional graded left $A$-module is a finite direct sum of
nonzero graded-indecomposable modules (modules not decomposable as a direct sum
of two nonzero graded submodules), with the zero module represented by the
empty sum. If a module has two such decompositions, their summands have the same
finite multiset of isomorphism classes in $\operatorname{GrMod}_0(A)$, that is,
up to degree-zero graded isomorphism
([[def-graded-ring-module-bimodule-and-internal-shift]]). Ungraded isomorphism
classes are not substituted.

derivations.claim: Let $L/K$ be a finite cyclic extension with generator $\sigma$ of order $r$, and let $T$ be a $\sigma$-semilinear automorphism of a finite $L$-space with $T^r=1$. Fixed vectors span it over $L$. Otherwise quotient by their $L$-span and choose $\bar v\ne0$ there. Every average $\sum_{j=0}^{r-1}T^j(a v)$ is fixed, so in the quotient $\sum_j\sigma^j(a)T^j\bar v=0$ for all $a\in L$. A coordinate functional nonzero on $\bar v$ contradicts [F2]. Choose an $L$-basis among the fixed vectors. A linear combination is fixed exactly when all its coefficients are fixed by $\sigma$, so these same vectors are a $K$-basis of the fixed space. This proves semilinear vector-space descent, and invariant arrow maps descend in these bases.

Suppose a geometric Schur class is fixed by $\operatorname{Fr}^m$. Choose a model and an intertwiner to its transform, all over a finite extension $L$ of $K=k_m$; enlarge $L$ if necessary so it is cyclic over $K$. The intertwiner defines a semilinear operator $T$ on the sum of the vertex spaces, preserving the vertex decomposition and commuting with all arrows. Its $r$th power is an endomorphism of the Schur representation, so is a common scalar $\lambda$. Commuting $T$ with $T^r$ gives $\sigma(\lambda)=\lambda$, hence $\lambda\in K^\times$. The norm $L^\times\to K^\times$ is onto: by [F1] it sends a cyclic generator to an element of order $|K^\times|$. Choose $a$ with norm $\lambda^{-1}$; then $(aT)^r=1$. Step 1.1 supplies fixed bases and a model over $K$. If two models over $K$ are geometrically isomorphic, their intertwiner space is the kernel of a matrix of linear equations over $K$, whose dimension stays $1$ after scalar extension. A nonzero rational intertwiner is therefore a scalar multiple over $\overline k$ of an isomorphism and is invertible. This proves uniqueness of the rational model.

A class fixed by $\operatorname{Fr}^m$ with orbit length less than $m$ is fixed by $\operatorname{Fr}^d$ for some proper divisor $d$ of $m$. For each $d$, step 2.1 places these fixed classes in bijection with a subset of the isomorphism classes of dimension-$\delta$ representations over $k_d$. There are finitely many such representations up to isomorphism: after fixing the finite bases, there are finitely many arrow-matrix tuples over the finite field $k_d$. Thus each fixed set for a small $d$ is finite, and we may increase $C$ to cover the finitely many small extension degrees. The number of classes with orbit length less than $m$ is at most $\sum_{d\mid m,d<m}Cq^d\le Cm q^{m/2}$. Thus at least $cq^m-Cm q^{m/2}\ge(c/2)q^m$ classes have exact orbit length $m$ for large $m$, yielding at least $(c/2)q^m/m$ distinct Frobenius orbits.

For a Schur representative over $k_m$ with exact orbit length $m$, restrict every vertex space and arrow to $k$. Such a representative exists by step 2.1. After scalar extension to $\overline k$, the resulting representation is the direct sum of its $m$ Frobenius conjugates: the algebra $k_m\otimes_k\overline k$ is the product of $m$ copies of $\overline k$ under its distinct embeddings, since the finite extension is separable. Each conjugate is indecomposable, because its endomorphism ring is a field, and they are pairwise nonisomorphic by exact orbit length. If the restricted representation split over $k$, its two nonzero summands would, by [F3], partition this multiset into two nonempty Frobenius-stable subsets. Frobenius acts transitively, so no such partition exists. Hence restriction is indecomposable. Two restrictions from distinct orbits cannot be isomorphic, again by their scalar-extended decompositions and [F3]. Nilpotence of all sufficiently long paths is preserved by restriction. Combining with step 3.1 gives the stated bound.

Let $Q$ be a finite quiver, $k=\mathbb F_q$, and $\overline k$ an algebraic
closure. A finite-dimensional representation $M$ over $\overline k$ is
called Schur here when $\operatorname{End}_{\overline k Q}M=\overline k$.
Let $\mathscr S$ be a Frobenius-stable set of Schur geometric isomorphism
classes of a fixed dimension vector $\delta$, consisting of representations
defined over some finite extensions. Every class fixed by the $m$th
Frobenius power has a model over $k_m=\mathbb F_{q^m}$, unique up to
$k_m$-isomorphism. If constants $c,C>0$ satisfy
$$c q^m\le|\operatorname{Fix}(\operatorname{Fr}^m;\mathscr S)|\le Cq^m$$
for all sufficiently large $m$, then for all sufficiently large $m$ there
are at least $c' q^m/m$ pairwise nonisomorphic indecomposable
$kQ$-representations of dimension $m\delta$, for a constant $c'>0$.
This conclusion also holds within the nilpotent representation category
when the classes in $\mathscr S$ are nilpotent.

Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from finite-root suppliers. Let $Q$ be a finite acyclic quiver and $k=\mathbb F_q$. At a sink $i$
define the reflection functor on a representation $M$ by replacing $M_i$ with
$\ker(\bigoplus_{j\to i}M_j\to M_i)$ and reversing the incident arrows
using its kernel projections. At a source use the dual cokernel functor.
These are inverse exact equivalences between the full subcategories with no
$S_i$ direct summand. They commute with field extension.

If the underlying graph is a finite ADE forest, the dimension map gives a bijection from the indecomposable $kQ$-modules
to the positive roots of the componentwise finite root system. Every
indecomposable is absolutely indecomposable, has endomorphism ring $k$ and
self-$\operatorname{Ext}^1=0$. There is an ordering $M_1,\ldots,M_m$ of
these indecomposables with
$$\operatorname{Hom}(M_j,M_i)=0,\qquad \operatorname{Ext}^1(M_i,M_j)=0\qquad(i<j).$$
Here representations are finite-dimensional; there are no oriented cycles,
so path nilpotence is automatic.

Let $(W,S)$ be a Coxeter system with $S$ finite, $|S|=n$, Coxeter diagram $\Gamma$, and Coxeter elements $c,c'$ defined as once-each products ([[def-cg-coxeter-diagram-components-and-finite-type]], [[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]], [[def-cg-coxeter-noncrossing-poset-and-kreweras-map]] (1)). Suppose $W$ is of finite type. Then every connected component of $\Gamma$ is a tree: finiteness of $W$ makes the Coxeter form $B$ positive definite, and its restriction to each component is positive definite ([[thm-cg-finite-type-positive-definite-criterion]] (1)); the positive-definite diagram exclusions show each component has no cycle ([[lem-cg-positive-definite-diagram-exclusions]] (2)); hence each nonempty connected component is a tree ([[def-tree-forest-and-leaf]]).

**(1) Orientation moves on a tree.** Let $T$ be a finite tree. A **source** in an orientation is a vertex whose incident arrows all point away from it; a **sink** is one whose incident arrows all point towards it. **Firing** a source or sink reverses all its incident arrows. Every orientation of $T$ is acyclic, and any two orientations are connected by a finite sequence of firings.

**(2) Orderings and orientations.** An ordering of $S$ orients each edge $\{s,t\}$ of $\Gamma$ from its earlier vertex to its later vertex. This orientation is acyclic, and every acyclic orientation is obtained from some ordering. Its product is independent of the chosen ordering that realizes the orientation, so an acyclic orientation determines a Coxeter element. If a source or sink $s$ is fired, the new Coxeter element is $s c s=s c s^{-1}$.

**(3) Conjugacy.** If every connected component of $\Gamma$ is a tree, then any two Coxeter elements are conjugate by a product of simple reflections. In particular this holds in finite type, since then every connected component is a tree. If $S=\emptyset$, then $W=\{1\}$ and the unique Coxeter element is conjugate to itself.

**(4) Limits.** Finite type is sufficient, not necessary, for the conjugacy assertion: its proof only needs each component to be a tree. No conjugacy claim is made for diagrams with cycles. No finite classification or geometric realization is used, and no Choice is needed.

For every $r$-subset $I$ of a basis of an $n$-dimensional $V$, the locus $p_I\ne0$ in $\operatorname{Gr}(r,V)$ is isomorphic to $\mathbf A_k^{r(n-r)}$; these loci cover the Grassmannian and have regular transition maps.
For $0\le r\le n$, $\operatorname{Gr}(r,V)$ is smooth in the elementary local-affine-chart sense, irreducible, and has dimension $r(n-r)$.

derivations.claim: For affine D, choose all arrows at the outer leaves pointing toward the central chain and choose any orientation of its edges. Take the chain spaces to have dimension $2$ and their maps to be isomorphisms; identify them along the chain. The four nonzero leaf maps then specify four lines in a common $2$-space. Isomorphisms of such representations are exactly common $\operatorname{GL}_2$ transports of the four lines, and their endomorphisms are exactly linear maps preserving all four lines. Three distinct lines force that endomorphism to be scalar: preserving two lines diagonalizes it and preserving a third with both coordinates nonzero equates the diagonal entries. Such configurations exist over an algebraic closure in every characteristic. Their variety $F=(\mathbb P^1)^4$ is irreducible of dimension $4=2^2$. The stated vector is a null vector: each leaf equation is $2\cdot1-2=0$, each interior chain equation is $2\cdot2-2-2=0$, and each end branch has $2\cdot2-2-1-1=0$; the one-vertex chain has four leaves and the same equality. It is primitive because it has entries $1$.

For affine E, orient all arms toward the center and take every arm map injective. Such representations modulo changes of bases on the arms are triples of flags in the central $N$-space, with steps $N/s,\ldots, (s-1)N/s$. Endomorphisms are exactly central endomorphisms preserving these flags, since an arm endomorphism is their unique restriction. The product flag variety $F$ is irreducible. The dimension of the flag for $s$ equal blocks of size $N/s$ is $\sum_{i<j}(N/s)^2=N^2(s-1)/(2s)$ by its successive graph charts. Thus $\dim F=N^2$, because $1/p+1/q+1/r=1$. Each internal null-vector equation is a second difference of this arithmetic progression; at the center it is $2N-N\sum_s(s-1)/s=0$. The vectors have entries with greatest common divisor $1$, proving that they are the primitive positive null vectors.

For E6 choose two opposite full flags in dimension $3$. Their common endomorphisms are diagonal. Choose the first line of the third full flag to be spanned by $(1,1,1)$ and extend it to any full flag. A diagonal endomorphism preserving this line has equal entries, so the common endomorphism algebra is scalar. For E7 choose two opposite full flags in dimension $4$. Choose the third, two-dimensional subspace to be spanned by $u=(1,1,1,1)$ and $v=(\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\lambda_3,\lambda_4)$ with four distinct $\lambda_i$ over the algebraic closure. If a diagonal matrix preserves this plane, its diagonal entries are $a+b\lambda_i$, while preservation of $v$ says $b\lambda_i^2+(a-d)\lambda_i-c=0$ for all four distinct $\lambda_i$. A quadratic polynomial cannot have four distinct roots unless zero, so $b=c=0$ and $d=a$. The matrix is scalar. These arguments hold in every characteristic.

For E8, choose a full flag in a $6$-space grouped into three consecutive pairs, and the opposite partial flag consisting of the last pair and last two pairs. An endomorphism preserving both is block diagonal with three upper triangular $2$-by-$2$ blocks: the full flag makes it upper triangular and the opposite partial flag eliminates the off-block entries. Choose three full flags $\ell_i\subset P_i$ in a $3$-space whose common endomorphisms are scalar, as in step 2.1. Map this space into $\bigoplus_{i=1}^3(k^3/\ell_i)$ by its three quotient maps; it is injective because the three lines have zero intersection. Identify the first coordinate line in each two-dimensional quotient with $P_i/\ell_i$. Use the image as the remaining three-dimensional subspace in the $6$-space. If the three upper triangular blocks preserve this image, they induce a common endomorphism $C$ of $k^3$; the quotient identities force $C$ to preserve every $\ell_i$ and $P_i$. Hence $C$ is scalar by step 2.1, and surjectivity of the quotient maps forces each block to be that same scalar. Thus E8 also has a configuration with scalar endomorphism algebra in every characteristic.

For each of these product flag varieties $F$, let $F^s$ be the locus of scalar endomorphism algebra. It is nonempty by steps 1.1, 2.1 and 3.1 and open: preservation of the flags is a finite linear system in the $N^2$ matrix entries; its kernel always contains the scalars, and has dimension $1$ exactly when some $(N^2-1)$-minor is nonzero. Every product flag variety has an affine big cell of dimension $N^2$ over $k$. Its intersection with $F^s$ is nonempty by irreducibility, so on that cell one such minor is a nonzero polynomial over $k$ of fixed degree. A nonzero degree-$D$ polynomial in $d$ variables has at most $DQ^{d-1}$ zeros over $\mathbb F_Q$, by induction on variables and the one-variable root bound. Therefore $|F^s(\mathbb F_Q)|\ge c_1Q^{N^2}$ for large $Q$. The full flag counts, or a finite cover by the standard cells [F4], give $|F(\mathbb F_Q)|\le c_2Q^{N^2}$. Every orbit in $F^s(\mathbb F_Q)$ has cardinality $|\operatorname{GL}_N(\mathbb F_Q)|/(Q-1)$, because its endomorphisms are exactly the scalars. By [F4] that orbit cardinality is bounded above and below by fixed positive constants times $Q^{N^2-1}$. Hence its number of rational orbits is bounded above and below by fixed positive constants times $Q$.

Let $\mathscr S$ be the geometric Schur classes of the representations just constructed, with the injection/isomorphism conditions on the arrows. These conditions are invariant under Frobenius and base extension. The finite-field descent lemma [F1] shows that Frobenius-fixed classes have rational models; all these rank conditions hold on that model because they hold after scalar extension. Two rational models in one geometric Schur class are rationally isomorphic by the same lemma. After normalizing the chain isomorphisms and forgetting the arm bases, their classes are precisely the rational flag orbits counted in step 4.1. Thus the fixed-class numbers are comparable to $q^m$, and [F1] gives the claimed exponential lower bound for the chosen orientations.

For an arbitrary orientation of the same tree, use a finite sequence of source/sink firings from [F3]. The null-vector equations checked in steps 1.1–1.2 imply $s_i\delta=\delta$ at every vertex. A $\delta$-dimensional indecomposable is never a vertex simple. The reflection equivalences [F2] therefore give bijections of Schur classes of dimension $\delta$ through the whole firing sequence. They commute with extension and Frobenius and hence preserve all fixed-class counts and exact Frobenius orbit lengths. Apply [F1] again to get the bound in the target orientation. Every path of length at least the number of vertices in a tree orientation is zero, so all constructed representations are nilpotent. This completes the full orientation and category assertions.
