Let $\mathcal A$ be a finite-field hereditary Hall category over
$\mathbb F_q$, and choose the positive square root $\nu=\sqrt q$. For
objects $M,N$, put
$\chi_0(M,N)=\dim_{\mathbb F_q}\operatorname{Hom}(M,N)-
\dim_{\mathbb F_q}\operatorname{YExt}^1(M,N)$. This integer depends only on
the isomorphism classes of $M,N$. At this point $\chi_0$ is only an
object-level exponent; additivity on $K_0$ and the resulting bicharacter are
separate proof obligations. The coefficient field is $\mathbb Q(\nu)$. The
**Euler-twisted Hall algebra** is the graded
vector
space
$$ H_{\mathcal A,\nu}=\bigoplus_{[M]}\mathbb Q(\nu)[M],\qquad \deg[M]=[M]\in K_0(\mathcal A), $$
with bilinear operation
$$ [M]\star[N] =\nu^{\chi_0(M,N)}\sum_{[L]}g^L_{M,N}[L], $$
where [[def-untwisted-hall-algebra]] fixes
$0\to N\to L\to M\to0$. This operation is distinct from the untwisted
product: its field, Euler exponent and square-root parameter are additional
data. Finite support and associativity are verified in the following items.

Let $\mathcal A$ be a finite-field hereditary Hall category and let
$K_0=K_0(\mathcal A)$. Put
$([\alpha],[\beta])=\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle+
\langle\beta,\alpha\rangle$. The **extended Hall algebra** is the vector
space $\widetilde H=\mathbb Q(\nu)[K_0]\otimes H_{\mathcal A,\nu}$ with
basis $k_\alpha[M]$ and multiplication
$$ (k_\alpha[M])(k_\beta[N]) =\nu^{-(\beta,[M])}k_{\alpha+\beta}([M]\star[N]). $$
The notation is left-torus normal order: $k_\alpha[M]$ is the actual product of the torus and Hall elements. Thus moving $k_\beta$ past $[M]$ contributes $\nu^{-(\beta,[M])}$. Equivalently, $k_\alpha k_\beta=k_{\alpha+\beta}$ and
$k_\alpha[M]k_\alpha^{-1}=\nu^{(\alpha,[M])}[M]$. Associativity follows
from the bilinearity of the symmetric Euler form and the associative Hall
product; the toral action is checked in
[[lem-extended-hall-torus-action-is-well-defined]].

If $\mathcal A$ has a specified set of simple objects $\{S_i\}$, the
**composition subalgebra** is the subalgebra of $H_{\mathcal A,\nu}$
generated by $[S_i]$. Its extension by all $k_\alpha$ is the **extended
composition subalgebra**.

Let $Q$ be any orientation of a finite ADE forest over $k=\mathbb F_q$,
with $\nu=\sqrt q>1$ and coefficient field $\mathbb Q(\nu)$.
Its Euler-twisted Hall algebra is generated by the vertex-simple classes.
Consequently its composition algebra equals the full positive Hall algebra,
and adjoining the declared Cartan torus gives the full extended Hall algebra.
No fixed-parameter quantum-group injectivity theorem or Hall polynomial
existence theorem is a premise.

Let $Q$ have underlying graph an affine tree of type
$\widetilde D_n$ ($n\ge4$), $\widetilde E_6$, $\widetilde E_7$ or
$\widetilde E_8$, with any orientation, over $k=\mathbb F_q$.
Let $\delta$ be its primitive positive null vector. There are constants
$c>0,m_0$ such that for every $m\ge m_0$ the category has at least
$cq^m/m$ pairwise nonisomorphic indecomposable representations of dimension
$m\delta$. All its representations are nilpotent, since the underlying
graph is a tree. The construction uses only partial flags, finite-field
descent and source/sink reflection, not a classification of arbitrary
quiver indecomposables.

For $\widetilde D$, $\delta$ has value $2$ along the central chain and
$1$ on its four outer leaves. For $\widetilde E$, use the star with arm
types $(p,q,r)=(3,3,3),(2,4,4),(2,3,6)$, respectively. The central value is
$N=3,4,6$, and the arm values, from the outside inward, are
$N/s,2N/s,\ldots,(s-1)N/s$ for an arm of type $s$.

Let $Q=p^a>1$, $\nu=\sqrt Q$, and $K=\mathbb Q(\nu)\subset\mathbb R$. Let $\mathcal H$ be the real twisted Hall algebra of the finite-dimensional nilpotent representations of a finite loopless quiver over $\mathbb F_Q$; an acyclic quiver needs no nilpotence restriction. Write $u_i=[S_i]$ for its vertex simples and $C_K$ for the $K$-algebra they generate. Let $A=\mathbb Z[t,t^{-1}]$, and let $U_A^-$ be the generic divided-power integral half for the symmetric matrix $a_{ij}=2\delta_{ij}-(\text{number of arrows joining }i,j)$.

There is a surjective graded algebra map
$$\Psi:K\otimes_{A,t\mapsto\nu^{-1}}U_A^-\longrightarrow C_K,\qquad F_i\longmapsto u_i.$$
It preserves the homogeneous form $(Q-1)^{-\operatorname{ht}\alpha}B_{\nu^{-1}}$. In particular $\dim_K C_K[\alpha]$ is at most the classical PBW rank. This conclusion requires only positive Green pairing and the generic word-form identity, and does not require specialized nondegeneracy or any numerical Serre-presentation comparison.

The roots of the untwisted affine algebra relative to $\widehat{\mathfrak h}$ are $\alpha+n\delta$ for finite roots $\alpha$ and $n\in\mathbb Z$, and $n\delta$ for $n\in\mathbb Z\setminus\{0\}$. The former are real of multiplicity one, with spaces $\mathfrak g_\alpha\otimes t^n$; the latter are imaginary of multiplicity $\ell=\dim\mathfrak h$, with spaces $\mathfrak h\otimes t^n$.

Let $L$ be a complex Lie algebra with a supplied finite or countable ordered basis $(x_i)$. The products $x_{i_1}\cdots x_{i_m}$ with $i_1\le\cdots\le i_m$, including $1$ for $m=0$, form a basis of $U(L)$. Consequently $L\to U(L)$ is injective. For the finite-word graded algebras here, compatible homogeneous bases of subalgebras and quotients can be obtained without AC.

derivations.claim: Restrict to a full induced subquiver on a vertex subset $I$. Objects of dimension supported on $I$ have zero vector spaces elsewhere, so their representations, flags, nilpotence and Euler factors are exactly those of the induced subquiver. A word in simples with this degree cannot involve a vertex outside $I$, since all simple degrees are nonnegative. Thus its Hall and composition homogeneous components agree with those of the subquiver. A proper composition component for an induced subquiver therefore proves properness for $Q$.

On an affine D or E subtree let $H_\delta$ be the positive total height of its null vector. There is a constant $C$ bounding the sum of root-space multiplicities at every total height: by [F5] each finite root $\alpha$ contributes at most one integer mode $n$ to a given height $\operatorname{ht}(\alpha)+nH_\delta$, and imaginary modes contribute at most the finite rank. PBW therefore bounds the total-height generating series of the classical positive enveloping algebra coefficientwise by $P(t)=\prod_{h\ge1}(1-t^h)^{-C}$. For $s>0$, $\log P(e^{-s})=C\sum_{j\ge1}1/[j(e^{sj}-1)] \le (C/s)\sum_{j\ge1}j^{-2}$. The series and rearrangements converge absolutely because their terms are positive and $e^{-s}<1$. A coefficient of height $L$ is at most $e^{sL}P(e^{-s})$; putting $s=L^{-1/2}$ gives a bound $\exp(C'\sqrt L)$ for a fixed $C'$. In particular the classical PBW rank in root degree $m\delta$ is at most $\exp(C''\sqrt m)$. By the surjective upper-bound input [F4], the same bound holds for the composition degree.

If two vertices have $r$ arrows one way and $s$ the other, with $r+s\ge2$, use degree $(1,1)$. Nilpotence forces at least one of the two scalar-arrow vectors to be zero: a nonzero scalar in each direction would give a nonzero arbitrarily repeatable two-cycle. Conversely either one-direction vector is nilpotent. Changes of vertex bases scale a nonzero vector by a common scalar, so the isomorphism classes are the zero representation and the two projective sets of nonzero vectors. Their number is $1+(q^r-1)/(q-1)+(q^s-1)/(q-1)>2$. The composition degree is spanned by the two simple words. Hence it is proper, with no quantum rank input.

Suppose the simple underlying graph contains a chordless cycle of length $n\ge3$. On that induced subquiver use dimension $1$ at every vertex. Each proper subset of the $n$ edges specifies a representation by setting those arrows to $1$ and the rest to zero. Its support is a forest, so it is nilpotent in every original orientation. The $2^n-1$ distinct zero/nonzero supports give distinct isomorphism classes. For two nonadjacent vertices an extension of one vertex simple by the other is supported only at those vertices and has no arrow coordinates, so it splits. Their Hom space is zero by disjoint support, their cross Euler values vanish, and the split sum has a unique subobject of either prescribed vertex-simple type. Thus both Hall products are the same direct-sum class, and nonadjacent vertex simples commute. Permutations of the $n$ letters modulo adjacent swaps of nonneighbors correspond to acyclic orientations of the cycle: orient an edge from its earlier letter to its later one. Every acyclic orientation has a topological ordering. Any two such orderings for it are linear extensions of the same partial order; move the first letter of one left in the other, crossing only incomparable letters, and induct to connect them by the allowed swaps. Exactly two of the $2^n$ edge orientations are cyclic. Thus the composition degree has dimension at most $2^n-2$, less than the Hall degree. This proves properness for every orientation, including the nilpotent oriented-cycle case.

It remains to classify connected simple trees not of finite ADE type. A vertex of degree at least $4$ contains the induced four-leaf star $\widetilde D_4$. If there are two vertices of degree $3$, choose a closest pair. Their joining path has no branch vertex inside; attach two outward neighbors at each end. The induced subgraph is an affine D tree with two branch vertices and four leaves. If there are no branch vertices, the tree is a path of type A. In the remaining case there is exactly one branch vertex of degree $3$, with three arms of lengths $p-1\le q-1\le r-1$, where $2\le p\le q\le r$. The cases $(2,2,r)$ and $(2,3,3),(2,3,4),(2,3,5)$ are precisely finite D and E; if $p\ge3$, truncating arms gives $(3,3,3)$; if $p=2,q\ge4$, it gives $(2,4,4)$; and if $p=2,q=3,r\ge6$, it gives $(2,3,6)$. These are respectively the affine E6,E7,E8 induced subtrees. Thus any remaining non-ADE tree contains an affine D or E induced subtree. An arbitrary graph either has the parallel-edge case, has an induced chordless cycle (take a shortest cycle), or is a forest to which this classification applies.

The Hall basis contains each of the pairwise nonisomorphic indecomposables from [F3], so its degree $m\delta$ has dimension at least $cq^m/m$. For large $m$ this exceeds $\exp(C''\sqrt m)$, since $m\log q-\log m-C''\sqrt m\to+\infty$. Hence composition is proper on the affine subtree. Steps 1.1 and 3.1, together with steps 2.1–2.2, prove properness whenever any component is not finite ADE. This argument used only the surjection in [F4], not an injection or an equality of quantum and Hall dimensions.

If every component is finite ADE, [F2] gives equality of composition and full Hall. Otherwise step 4.1 gives properness in a supported degree. The torus extension is a direct sum of its declared toral normal-form copies of the positive Hall algebra, so adjoining the torus neither removes nor creates the difference between these positive subspaces. This proves the entire componentwise criterion and its extended version.

derivations.claim: First define $D,D'$ on the free algebra by the displayed word rules. Write $e=e_i$. Both operators lower the number of letters $e$ in a word by one, so are locally nilpotent there. For each Serre polynomial on letters $e_j,e_k$, put $r=1-a_{jk}$. If $i$ is distinct from $j,k$, its image under $D$ is zero. If $i=j$, set $a=a_{jk}=1-r$. The two terms in $D(e^{r-s}e_ke^s)$ have respective coefficients $q^{r-s-1}[r-s]_q$ and $q^{2(r-s)+a+s-1}[s]_q$ on the words with the appropriate one fewer $e$. On a fixed resulting word $e^{r-s-1}e_ke^s$, the contributions from indices $s$ and $s+1$ cancel: their common $q$-power is $q^{r-s-1}$ and their remaining coefficients cancel by [F1]. If $i=k$, removing its single letter gives $e_j^r$ times $\sum_s(-1)^s{r\brack s}_q q^{a_{ij}(r-s)}$. Symmetry gives $a_{ij}=a_{kj}=a_{jk}=1-r$, so this sum is zero by [F1]. Thus $D$ kills every generating Serre polynomial. Its skew product rule then preserves their two-sided ideal, so it descends to $S$. Reversing word order interchanges $D,D'$ and preserves that ideal, since reversal multiplies each Serre polynomial by $(-1)^r$. Hence $D'$ also descends. The degree-lowering argument proves local nilpotence on $S$.

The operators commute. To check this without any presentation comparison, induct on word length in the free algebra. For homogeneous words $x,y$ of $i$-weights $m_x,m_y$, both $DD'(xy)$ and $D'D(xy)$ expand to $q^{m_y}DD'(x)y+D(x)D'(y)+q^{m_x+m_y-2}D'(x)D(y)+q^{m_x}xDD'(y)$, using the inductive commutation on $x,y$. They agree on generators, so agree on all words and on $S$. In particular $D'$ preserves $B_i$. The skew product rule shows that $B_i$ is a graded subalgebra.

For homogeneous $b\in B_i$ of $i$-weight $m$, $D(eb)=b$ and $D(be)=q^m b$, so $R(b)=eb-q^{-m}be$ belongs to $B_i$. For homogeneous $b,c\in B_i$ one has $R(bc)=R(b)c+q^{-m_b}bR(c)$. Moreover direct application of the second skew rule gives $D'(R(b))=(q^m-q^{-m})b+R(D'(b))$, since $D'(b)$ has weight $m-2$. With $F=-D'/(q-q^{-1})$, this is $RF(b)-FR(b)=[m]_q b$. The grading gives $KRK^{-1}=q^2R$ and $KFK^{-1}=q^{-2}F$, and $K$ is invertible. Thus these operators satisfy every defining relation of $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ on $B_i$. Their product rules are $R(bc)=R(b)c+K^{-1}(b)R(c)$, $F(bc)=F(b)K(c)+bF(c)$, and $K(bc)=K(b)K(c)$.

For $j\ne i$ put $N=-a_{ij}$. Iterating the definition of $R$ gives $R^r(e_j)=\sum_{s=0}^r(-1)^s q^{-s(a_{ij}+r-1)}{r\brack s}_q e^{r-s}e_je^s.$ Indeed the case $r=0$ is immediate, and passing from $r$ to $r+1$ uses $R(R^r e_j)=eR^r e_j-q^{-a_{ij}-2r}(R^r e_j)e$ and the quantum-binomial recurrence. At $r=N+1$ the extra $q$-factor is $1$, so the numerical Serre relation is exactly $R^{N+1}(e_j)=0$. Since $F(e_j)=0$ and its weight is $-N$, the commutator in step 3.1 gives by induction $F(R^r e_j)=[r]_q[N-r+1]_qR^{r-1}e_j$ for $r\geq1$. The needed scalar identity is $\sum_{t=0}^{r-1}[m+2t]_q=[r]_q[m+r-1]_q$, obtained by summing the defining geometric series. Therefore $V_j=\operatorname{span}\{R^r(e_j):0\leq r\leq N\}$ is a finite-dimensional invariant subspace with weights $-N,-N+2,\ldots,N$.

Let $B_0$ be the subalgebra generated by all these $V_j$, $j\ne i$. It is contained in $B_i$ and stable under $R$, by its product rule and the terminating strings of step 4.1. The normal-order identity $be=q^m eb-q^mR(b)$ for homogeneous $b\in B_0$ shows that $\sum_{n\geq0}e^nB_0$ is stable under right multiplication by $e$. It is also stable under right multiplication by every $e_j$ with $j\ne i$, since these lie in $B_0$. It contains $1$, hence every word in the generators and all of $S$. Thus $S=\sum_{n\geq0}e^nB_0$.

This sum is direct. For $b\in B_i$, iterating $D$ gives $D(e^n b)=q^{n-1}[n]_q e^{n-1}b$ and $D^n(e^n b)=q^{n(n-1)/2}[n]_q!b$. If $\sum_{n=0}^d e^n b_n=0$ with $b_n\in B_i$ and $b_d\ne0$, application of $D^d$ gives $q^{d(d-1)/2}[d]_q!b_d=0$, impossible by [F1]. Consequently the expression in step 5.1 is unique. Applying $D$ to that expression and using the directness just proved shows that an element in $\ker D$ has $b_n=0$ for every $n>0$. Hence $B_i=B_0$, and rescaling $e^n$ by the nonzero $[n]_q!$ gives the asserted divided-power direct sum.

The action on $B_i$ is integrable. Each $V_j$ in step 4.1 is finite-dimensional with a finite set of integer weights, so its raising and lowering operators are nilpotent. The product formulas of step 3.1 make multiplication $V_{j_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes V_{j_t}\to B_i$ equivariant for the coproducts $\Delta(R)=R\otimes1+K^{-1}\otimes R$, $\Delta(F)=F\otimes K+1\otimes F$, $\Delta(K)=K\otimes K$. These coproduct formulas satisfy the same rank-one relations, as is verified directly using $KR=q^2RK$ and $KF=q^{-2}FK$. Each finite tensor product has only finitely many weights; $R$ increases weight by two and $F$ decreases it by two, so both are nilpotent on it. Every element of $B_i=B_0$ is a finite sum of products of root-string generators, hence lies in a finite sum of such invariant images. Thus $R,F$ are locally nilpotent and $K$ acts with eigenvalues $q^m$, $m\in\mathbb Z$. No complete reducibility theorem for rank-one representations is used.

Finally let $0\ne z\in S_\beta$ satisfy $D(z)=D'(z)=0$, and put $m=m(\beta)$. Then $z\in B_i$ and $Fz=0$. By step 7.1 there is an integer $n\geq0$ with $R^n z\ne0$ and $R^{n+1}z=0$. Since $q>1$, this forces $m=-n\leq0$, as required.

Assume the inherited Axiom of Choice of the global-basis suppliers. Let $I$ be a finite symmetric Cartan datum with symmetrizers $d_i=1$; its generalized Cartan matrix need not be of finite type. Write $A=\mathbb Z[t,t^{-1}]$, and let $U_A^-$ denote the divided-power integral half inside the generic quantum Serre algebra over $\mathbb Q(t)$. Let $Q=p^a>1$ be a prime power, let $\nu=\sqrt Q>1$, and set $K=\mathbb Q(\nu)$ and $H_\pm=K\otimes_{A,t\mapsto\nu^{\pm1}}U_A^-$.

The normalized Kashiwara form $B_t$ specializes to a nondegenerate symmetric form on every finite homogeneous component of both $H_+$ and $H_-$. Their component dimensions are the classical PBW ranks. On $H_-$ the primitive-generator coproduct has tensor multiplication
$$ (x\otimes y)(x'\otimes y')=\nu^{(\deg y,\deg x')}xx'\otimes yy'. $$
The rescaled homogeneous form $G(x,y)=(Q-1)^{-\operatorname{ht}\alpha}B_{\nu^{-1}}(x,y)$ for $x,y\in H_-[-\alpha]$, zero in different degrees, has $G(F_i,F_j)=\delta_{ij}/(Q-1)$ and both braided Hopf adjunctions. Thus it has exactly the generator values and symmetric tensor twist of the Green pairing.

This statement concerns the specialization of the integral half. It does not identify that algebra with the algebra presented at the numerical parameter by the quantum Serre relations alone.

Let $\psi$ (the bar involution) and $\tau$ (the contravariant anti-involution) be
the semilinear maps of
[[lem-quantum-serre-relations-are-stable-under-the-chevalley-involutions]], so
that $\psi(q)=q^{-1}$, $\psi(E_i)=E_i$, $\psi(F_i)=F_i$, $\psi(K_h)=K_h^{-1}$
and $\tau(q)=q^{-1}$, $\tau(E_i)=F_i$, $\tau(F_i)=E_i$, $\tau(K_h)=K_h^{-1}$,
with $\tau$ anti-multiplicative. Let $A=\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$ and let $U_A$ be
the Lusztig divided-power integral form with its generators $E_i^{(r)}$,
$F_i^{(r)}$, $K_h^{\pm1}$ and toral binomials $T_{i,c,t}$
([[def-lusztig-divided-power-integral-form]]). Then $\psi(U_A)=U_A$ and
$\tau(U_A)=U_A$. Explicitly, on the generators,

$$\psi(E_i^{(r)})=E_i^{(r)},\quad \psi(F_i^{(r)})=F_i^{(r)},\quad \psi(K_h)=K_h^{-1},\quad \psi(T_{i,c,t})=T_{i,c,t},$$

$$\tau(E_i^{(r)})=F_i^{(r)},\quad \tau(F_i^{(r)})=E_i^{(r)},\quad \tau(K_h)=K_h^{-1},\quad \tau(T_{i,c,t})=T_{i,c,t}.$$

In particular both maps restrict to bijections of $U_A$: $\psi$ to a semilinear
algebra involution of $U_A$ and $\tau$ to a semilinear anti-involution of
$U_A$, while $q^{\pm1}\in A$ keeps all coefficients in $A$. These are the two
involutions under which the bar lattice and the contravariant duality of the
later constructions are taken; neither formula is the Chevalley involution
$\omega$, which changes signs, exchanges the two halves and is treated in
[[lem-quantum-serre-relations-are-stable-under-the-chevalley-involutions]].
No choice is used.

derivations.claim: First the specialization has the usual triangular factors. At $\nu>1$ every quantum integer factorial and every toral-binomial denominator $\prod_{r=1}^n(t^r-t^{-r})$ is nonzero. Hence every specialized divided power and toral binomial is a scalar multiple of a polynomial in the undivided root generators and the group-like torus. Conversely the torus remains precisely its group algebra: for one simple direction the integral toral basis $K^\delta T_{0,r}$, $\delta\in\{0,1\}$, is Laurent triangular, since $T_{0,r}$ has powers $K^r,K^{r-2},\ldots,K^{-r}$ with nonzero extreme coefficients; ordered by the new extreme powers, this is an invertible triangular change of basis with all coefficients evaluable at $\nu$. Tensor the finitely many simple directions and the unchanged lattice-coset representatives. Together with [F1], this proves $U\cong U^-\otimes K[P^\vee]\otimes U^+$ as a vector space. In particular $M_U(\lambda)=U^-v_\lambda$ has the expected free half coordinates for every integral label $\lambda$. This uses only actual integral specialization.

Transport the generic library algebra to the displayed source convention by $q\mapsto t^{-1}$, $E_i^{\mathrm{lib}}\mapsto F_i$, $F_i^{\mathrm{lib}}\mapsto E_i$, and $K_h^{\mathrm{lib}}\mapsto K_h$. The toral actions hold because the root signs and parameter are both inverted. The mixed relation changes sign in both its commutator and its denominator. Symmetric quantum integers are invariant under parameter inversion, so every Serre relation is preserved. The library coproducts become exactly those in the statement. Thus [F2] transports to a generic tensor $\Theta=\sum_\gamma\Theta_\gamma$ with $\Theta_\gamma\in U^-[-\gamma]\otimes U^+[\gamma]$ and source identity $\Delta(u)\Theta=\Theta\bar\Delta(u)$, where $\bar\Delta E_i=E_i\otimes1+K_i^{-1}\otimes E_i$ and $\bar\Delta F_i=F_i\otimes K_i+1\otimes F_i$. This transported tensor is normalized by $\Theta_0=1$.

Each transported coefficient is regular at $t=\nu$: in global bases its construction in [F2] uses inverses of homogeneous Gram matrices, quantum factorials and nonzero generator normalization scalars. By [F1] the Gram matrices at $q=\nu^{-1}$ are invertible, and every other displayed denominator is nonzero. Thus every finite-degree tensor identity of step 1.2 can be evaluated, yielding a well-defined specialized $\Theta$ satisfying the same identities on the actual $U$. This is an evaluation of established identities at a separately proved nondegenerate value, not an assumption that a generic nonzero determinant remains nonzero.

Write $\Theta_\gamma=\sum_a a_{\gamma,a}\otimes b_{\gamma,a}$, in negative and positive degrees respectively, and define $\Omega=\sum_{\gamma,a}S(a_{\gamma,a})b_{\gamma,a}$. On any vector of label $\lambda$ in the stipulated module this is a finite sum: a nonzero $b_{\gamma,a}v$ requires $\lambda+\gamma$ in the bounded-above support, bounding the height of $\gamma$. Apply $m(S\otimes1)$ to the source $E_i$ intertwining identity from step 2.1. The two terms on its left cancel, because $S(E_i)=-K_i^{-1}E_i$. The terms on its right are $-K_i^{-1}E_i\Omega+K_i\Omega E_i$. Hence $K_i^{-1}E_i\Omega=K_i\Omega E_i$. For $F_i$, the two left terms cancel because $S(F_i)=-F_iK_i$, leaving $-F_iK_i\Omega K_i+\Omega F_i=0$. Toral weight zero gives $K_h\Omega=\Omega K_h$. These computations can first be truncated in root height; all boundary terms contain a positive-degree factor of height tending to infinity acting on $v$, $E_iv$ or $F_iv$ and vanish for a sufficiently large truncation. Therefore the operator identities are valid on every vector.

For a homogeneous vector $v$ of label $\lambda\in Q$, set $\mathcal C(v)=
u^{f(\lambda)}\Omega v$. Since $(\alpha_i,\alpha_i)=2$, $f(\lambda)-f(\lambda-\alpha_i)=2(\lambda,\alpha_i)$. The $E_i$ identity of step 3.1 says $E_i\Omega v=
u^{2(\lambda+\alpha_i,\alpha_i)}\Omega E_iv$, which, with $f(\lambda+\alpha_i)-f(\lambda)=2(\lambda+\alpha_i,\alpha_i)$, gives $\mathcal C E_i=E_i\mathcal C$. The $F_i$ identity says $F_i\Omega v=
u^{-2(\lambda,\alpha_i)}\Omega F_iv$, giving the other commutation by the first difference formula. The toral identity handles all group-likes. Thus $\mathcal C$ commutes with $U$, is natural for graded module maps and descends to subquotients. If $v_\lambda$ is highest, all positive-height $b_{\gamma,a}$ kill it, and $\Theta_0=1$ gives $\Omega v_\lambda=v_\lambda$. Hence $\mathcal C$ is $
u^{f(\lambda)}$ on its cyclic module.

For $\lambda=-\alpha_i$, $f(\lambda)=2-2=0$, so $\mathcal C=1$ on $M_U(-\alpha_i)$, its finite direct sum over $I$, and every graded subquotient. A nonzero highest vector of weight $-\beta$ in such a subquotient also has eigenvalue $\nu^{f(-\beta)}$ by step 4.1. Since $\nu>1$ and $f(-\beta)$ is an integer, equality with $1$ implies $f(-\beta)=0$, namely $(\beta,\beta)=2\operatorname{ht}\beta$. This proves all claims.

Let $\widetilde U$ be the algebra generated by all $E_i,F_i,K_h$ with the toral, toral-action and mixed relations, and no relations within either root half. For every integral label $\lambda$, its universal highest module is freely based by $T v_\lambda$. To verify this without a presentation freeness assumption, define $F_i$ by left concatenation, $K_h$ on the word of degree $-\gamma$ by $
u^{\langle\lambda-\gamma,hangle}$, and, for $w=F_{i_1}\cdots F_{i_n}$, define $E_jwv_\lambda$ to be the sum over $r$ with $i_r=j$ of $[\langle\lambda-\sum_{s>r}\alpha_{i_s},h_jangle]_
u$ times the word with its $r$th letter deleted. The deletion formula satisfies $E_iF_jw=F_jE_iw+\delta_{ij}(K_i-K_i^{-1})w/(
u-
u^{-1})$; its labels verify both toral action relations. There are no further root-half relations to check. Thus these are $\widetilde U$-modules. Conversely the crossing relations move every positive and toral letter to the right in a highest module, so negative words span; the displayed representation makes them independent and proves the universal property. Denote this module by $\widetilde M(\lambda)$.

The actual algebra $U$ is a quotient of $\widetilde U$: by [F1] its undivided roots and torus generate it and satisfy all the required mixed and toral relations. The canonical module map $\widetilde M(\lambda)\to M_U(\lambda)$ is, on negative coordinates, exactly $T\to U^-$. Its kernel is consequently $Jv_\lambda$ for every $\lambda$, so this subspace is a $\widetilde U$-submodule. At $\lambda=0$ the augmentation subspace $T_+v_0$ is also a submodule: the deletion formula cannot produce a scalar except from a single letter, whose coefficient is $[0]_\nu=0$. Each $F_iv_0$ is highest of label $-\alpha_i$. Therefore the maps $\widetilde M(-\alpha_i)\to T_+v_0$, $v_{-\alpha_i}\mapsto F_iv_0$, are module maps, and their direct sum is an isomorphism because $T_+=\bigoplus_iTF_i$ is the unique last-letter decomposition.

Induce that direct sum along $\widetilde U\to U$. The universal property, or the mutually inverse maps $u\otimes(av_\lambda)\mapsto ua v_\lambda$ and $a v_\lambda\mapsto a\otimes v_\lambda$, gives $V:=U\otimes_{\widetilde U}(T_+v_0)\cong\bigoplus_iM_U(-\alpha_i)$. Define $\ell:J\to V$ by $\ell(a)=1\otimes av_0$. Since $Jv_0$ is a submodule by step 2.1, its image $\ell(J)$ is a $U$-submodule of $V$. For $a=\sum_i u_iF_i$, the direct-sum coordinates of $\ell(a)$ are $(\pi(u_i)v_{-\alpha_i})_i$. By [F1], this is zero if and only if each $u_i\in J$. Consequently $\ker\ell=\sum_iJF_i=JT_+$; the last equality follows by splitting the last letter of a nonempty right factor and using that $J$ is a two-sided ideal. No flatness of tensor induction was assumed: its kernel is computed directly in the known Verma coordinates.

The subspace $Sv_0$ is a $\widetilde U$-submodule. Multiplication by a negative generator and toral action preserve it. For a positive generator, the specialized opposite-Serre commutator of [F2] vanishes on every Serre generator $s$. Expanding $[E_i,a s b]=[E_i,a]s b+a s[E_i,b]$ leaves a Serre factor in each term; moving its toral factors across this homogeneous factor multiplies it only by a scalar. The deletion formula therefore sends $Sv_0$ into itself. It follows that $\ell(S)$ is a $U$-submodule of $V$, contained in $\ell(J)$, and $\ell(J)/\ell(S)$ is a submodule of $V/\ell(S)$. By [F1], the Casimir acts by $1$ throughout this quotient.

Choose $a\in J[-\beta]$ with $a\notin S$. Its image $\ell(a)+\ell(S)$ is nonzero. Otherwise $a-s\in\ker\ell=JT_+$ for a homogeneous $s\in S[-\beta]$; writing $a-s=\sum_i u_iF_i$ gives $u_i\in J[-\beta+\alpha_i]$ of smaller height, hence $u_i\in S$ by minimality. Degree zero and every pure simple-root polynomial component survive $T\to U^-$ by the integral rank-one half, so in particular $\beta\ne0$; its positive height makes the right side strictly positive. cycles, take the abelian category of finite-dimensional nilpotent
representations; if $Q$ is acyclic, take all finite-dimensional
representations. This category is a small finite-field hereditary Hall
category. Its simple objects are $S_i$, $K_0\cong\mathbb Z^{Q_0}$ by dimension
vector, and $\dim_{\mathbb F_q}\operatorname{YExt}^1(S_i,S_j)=c_{ij}$ for
arrows $i\to j$.

For a finite loopless quiver $Q$ over $\mathbb F_q$, using nilpotent
finite-dimensional representations when $Q$ has oriented cycles, the
assignment
$$ E_i\longmapsto[S_i],\qquad K_i^{\pm1}\longmapsto k_{\pm e_i} $$
defines a surjective bialgebra homomorphism from the extended positive Borel
of [[def-quiver-hall-positive-borel]] onto the extended composition
subalgebra of [[def-extended-hall-algebra-and-composition-subalgebra]]. The
claim does not include injectivity.

Let $Q=p^a>1$, $\nu=\sqrt Q$, and $K=\mathbb Q(\nu)\subset\mathbb R$. Let $\mathcal H$ be the real twisted Hall algebra of the finite-dimensional nilpotent representations of a finite loopless quiver over $\mathbb F_Q$; an acyclic quiver needs no nilpotence restriction. Write $u_i=[S_i]$ for its vertex simples and $C_K$ for the $K$-algebra they generate. Let $A=\mathbb Z[t,t^{-1}]$, and let $U_A^-$ be the generic divided-power integral half for the symmetric matrix $a_{ij}=2\delta_{ij}-(\text{number of arrows joining }i,j)$.

There is a surjective graded algebra map
$$\Psi:K\otimes_{A,t\mapsto\nu^{-1}}U_A^-\longrightarrow C_K,\qquad F_i\longmapsto u_i.$$
It preserves the homogeneous form $(Q-1)^{-\operatorname{ht}\alpha}B_{\nu^{-1}}$. In particular $\dim_K C_K[\alpha]$ is at most the classical PBW rank. This conclusion requires only positive Green pairing and the generic word-form identity, and does not require specialized nondegeneracy or any numerical Serre-presentation comparison.

On the direct-sum Hall space define
$$ ([M],[N])_G=\frac{\delta_{[M],[N]}}{a_M}. $$
This bilinear form is nondegenerate over $\mathbb Q(\nu)$ and satisfies
$$ ([M]\star[N],[R])_G =([M]\otimes[N],\Delta'([R]))_{G\otimes G}, $$
where the tensor pairing is the product of the two Green pairings.

Let $Q$ be a finite loopless quiver over $k=\mathbb F_q$, using
finite-dimensional nilpotent representations when oriented cycles occur,
and use the Euler-twisted Hall algebra over $\mathbb Q(\sqrt q)$.
Its vertex-simple-generated composition subalgebra equals the full Hall
algebra if and only if every connected component of the underlying
multigraph is a finite ADE Dynkin diagram. Thus adjoining the declared
Cartan torus gives the full extended Hall algebra exactly under the same
componentwise finite-type condition. The empty quiver is included.

No injectivity theorem for the Ringel map is a premise. The only quantum
rank input is the independent surjection from the specialized divided-power
integral half onto the composition algebra, which supplies an upper bound
by classical PBW ranks.

Let $Q$ be a finite loopless quiver over $\mathbb F_q$. Write $c_{ij}$ for
the number of arrows $i\to j$, set $\nu=\sqrt q>1$, and define the symmetric
Cartan matrix
$$ a_{ij}=2\delta_{ij}-c_{ij}-c_{ji}. $$
Let $\mathbb Q(\nu)$ be the coefficient field. Define the **extended
positive Borel algebra** $B_Q^+$ to be the $\mathbb Q(\nu)$-algebra generated
by $E_i$ and invertible commuting $K_i^{\pm1}$, with
$$ K_iK_i^{-1}=1, \qquad K_i E_jK_i^{-1}=\nu^{a_{ij}}E_j, $$
and, for $i\ne j$ and $m=1-a_{ij}$,
$$ \sum_{r=0}^{m}(-1)^r\binom{m}{r}_{\nu} E_i^{m-r}E_jE_i^r=0. $$
The Gaussian coefficients use the symmetric convention of
[[def-quantum-integers-factorials-and-divided-powers-at-q-i]]. The formulas
$$ \Delta(E_i)=E_i\otimes K_i^{-1}+1\otimes E_i, \qquad \Delta(K_i)=K_i\otimes K_i, $$
are the coproduct convention intended for this presentation; their
well-definedness on the defining relations is checked using
[[lem-coproduct-preserves-the-positive-and-negative-quantum-serre-ideals]].
The positive half is
the subalgebra generated by the $E_i$ alone; adjoining the $K_i^{\pm1}$ gives
the extended positive Borel.

Let $\mathcal A$ be a finite-field hereditary Hall category and let
$K_0=K_0(\mathcal A)$. Put
$([\alpha],[\beta])=\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle+
\langle\beta,\alpha\rangle$. The **extended Hall algebra** is the vector
space $\widetilde H=\mathbb Q(\nu)[K_0]\otimes H_{\mathcal A,\nu}$ with
basis $k_\alpha[M]$ and multiplication
$$ (k_\alpha[M])(k_\beta[N]) =\nu^{-(\beta,[M])}k_{\alpha+\beta}([M]\star[N]). $$
The notation is left-torus normal order: $k_\alpha[M]$ is the actual product of the torus and Hall elements. Thus moving $k_\beta$ past $[M]$ contributes $\nu^{-(\beta,[M])}$. Equivalently, $k_\alpha k_\beta=k_{\alpha+\beta}$ and
$k_\alpha[M]k_\alpha^{-1}=\nu^{(\alpha,[M])}[M]$. Associativity follows
from the bilinearity of the symmetric Euler form and the associative Hall
product; the toral action is checked in
[[lem-extended-hall-torus-action-is-well-defined]].

If $\mathcal A$ has a specified set of simple objects $\{S_i\}$, the
**composition subalgebra** is the subalgebra of $H_{\mathcal A,\nu}$
generated by $[S_i]$. Its extension by all $k_\alpha$ is the **extended
composition subalgebra**.

u$. Indeed, homogeneity of the Serre relations makes $x\mapsto
u^{(\alpha,\deg x)}x$ an automorphism of $S_
u$ for every $\alpha$; on the displayed vector space define $(K_\alpha x)(K_ eta y)=
